docs.title: Machine Learning — EGEI
docs.text: Learn the foundations of machine learning while working the way data teams actually work today: side by side with an AI coding assistant. You will not just prompt it — you will read, test and defend every line it writes.

docs.title: What this course is about
docs.text:
Machine learning has two halves. One is statistical: what a model is, what it can and cannot learn from data, and how to tell a real signal from noise. The other is craft: turning a business question into data, code and a decision someone can act on.

This year the craft half changes. Writing code is no longer the bottleneck — reviewing it is. So every session pairs a modelling topic with the corresponding assistant skill: how to ask for the right thing, how to check the answer, and how to recognise when the assistant is confidently wrong.

docs.title: Modelling foundations
docs.text: Regression, classification, resampling, trees, regularization and clustering, all on one real policy problem, with emphasis on why a model works, not only on calling .fit().

docs.title: Assistant-driven workflow
docs.text: Use Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor as a pair programmer: scaffolding, refactoring, debugging and explaining code — under a verification discipline you can defend.

docs.title: One real project
docs.text: Everything is assessed through one end-to-end project on real data, in two deliveries, with code, a written report and a live presentation.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the course you will be able to:

  1. Frame a business question as a supervised learning problem, and say what a good answer looks like.
  2. Prepare, explore and visualize a real dataset in Python, reproducibly.
  3. Choose, fit and tune regression and classification models, and justify the choice.
  4. Evaluate models honestly: train/test discipline, cross-validation, uncertainty and the right metric.
  5. Work with an AI coding assistant productively — and verify its output rather than trusting it.
  6. Communicate results and limitations to a non-technical audience.

docs.title: The Case: Who Should Get the Subsidy?
docs.text:
The thread that runs through every session Data: CASEN 2022 · Chile

Every session in this course works on the same problem and the same data. Each new method answers the next question that problem raises, and nothing gets used before it has been taught.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Governments in emerging economies spend a large share of their social budget on programmes targeted at poor households. To target, you need to know who is poor, and that usually means income. But income is hard to observe: much of it is informal, people have reasons to under-report it, and verifying it household by household is expensive.

The standard answer is a proxy means test: predict a household's welfare from characteristics that are easy to observe and hard to fake, such as schooling, household size, type of dwelling or health insurance. Chile's Registro Social de Hogares, Mexico's Progresa/Prospera and many World Bank–supported programmes use versions of this idea.

That is a machine learning problem, with all of its difficulties:

Question Where we meet it What kind of data do we have about a household? Session 1 · Data types How do we build one clean row per household? Session 2 · Data manipulation Can we predict income from what we observe? How wrong are we? Session 3 · ML models Is the error we report honest, or did we fool ourselves? Session 4 · The ML pipeline Who is poor? Which mistakes matter more? Session 5 · Classification Can more flexible models do better, and at what cost? Session 6 · Trees and ensembles Which variables do we really need? Session 7 · Selection and shrinkage What types of households are there, without labels? Session 8 · PCA and clustering

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
CASEN (Encuesta de Caracterización Socioeconómica Nacional) is Chile's main household survey, run by the Ministry of Social Development and Family. The 2022 round interviewed about 72,000 households. We use a random sample of 15,000 households, one row each, built from the record of the head of household.

⬇️ Download casen_households.csv

import pandas as pd
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/machine_learning_egei/main/docs/data/casen_households.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)

docs.title: Data dictionary
docs.text:
Column Type Description household_id id Course identifier (not the CASEN folio) region nominal Region of residence (16 regions) area nominal urban / rural head_sex nominal Sex of the head of household head_age continuous Age of the head of household head_schooling_years discrete Years of schooling of the head (missing = doesn't know) head_education ordinal Highest level reached, 0_none … 6_tertiary_complete head_activity nominal employed / unemployed / inactive head_job_type nominal Type of job; missing when the head does not work head_weekly_hours continuous Usual weekly hours; missing when the head does not work, and for 87 employed heads who did not know health_insurance nominal fonasa (public), isapre (private), armed_forces, none, other head_nationality nominal chilean / dual / foreign head_indigenous nominal Belongs to an indigenous people (yes / no) household_size discrete Number of people in the household has_children, has_elderly binary Anyone under 18 / over 60 in the household household_type nominal Single person, nuclear, extended, … overcrowding ordinal People per bedroom, 0_none … 3_critical housing_tenure nominal owned / rented / lent / irregular dwelling_type nominal house / apartment / precarious household_income continuous ⚠️ Total household income, CLP per month income_per_capita continuous ⚠️ Total income per person, CLP per month income_decile ordinal ⚠️ National income decile (1 = poorest) poor target 1 if the household is in income poverty survey_weight weight Expansion factor (how many households each row represents)

The ⚠️ columns: target in one task, leak in another

Income is the target when we predict income (Sessions 3–4). When we predict poverty (Session 5 onwards), income is off limits: poverty is defined from income per capita, and the whole point of a proxy means test is that income is not observed. A model that uses it scores brilliantly and is useless. Learning to spot this is part of the course.

Two things to know about the numbers

  • Poverty measure. poor uses the updated poverty methodology published in the current CASEN 2022 database: 23% of households in our sample and about 20% of people (weighted) are poor. Under the old 2013 methodology the official 2022 figure was 6.5%.
  • Weights. CASEN is a complex survey. For official statistics you would use survey_weight. For our prediction exercises we treat each household as one example; when a result is meant to describe Chile as a whole, we say so and weight it.

Source: Ministerio de Desarrollo Social y Familia, Encuesta CASEN 2022, current Stata database (data catalogue). The sample is rebuilt with scripts/build_casen_sample.py in the course repository.

docs.title: Working with a Code Assistant
docs.text:
Transversal thread of the course Required in every project delivery

An AI coding assistant will write most of the syntax you need this term. That is fine — it is how data teams work now. What it does not do is take responsibility for the result. This page is the working agreement for that: how to set it up, how to ask well, how to verify, and what you must disclose.

docs.title: 1. Pick one and set it up
docs.text:
Any of these is acceptable. Free tiers are enough for everything we do.

Tool Where it lives Good for Setup GitHub Copilot Inside VS Code / JetBrains Inline completion while you type Free for students via GitHub Education Claude Web chat, or in an editor Explaining and reviewing longer code and notebooks claude.ai ChatGPT Web chat; Advanced Data Analysis runs code Exploring a dataset end to end in one conversation chatgpt.com Gemini Web chat; also inside Colab Working directly in a Colab notebook gemini.google.com Cursor A full editor Refactoring across several files cursor.com

If you work in Google Colab

Colab has an assistant built in, so you need no local setup at all. In class we work in VS Code (set up in Session 1), but every session notebook also opens in Colab with one click.

docs.title: 2. Ask well: four things every prompt needs
docs.text:
A vague prompt produces code that runs and answers the wrong question. Include:

Element Bad Good Data "my dataframe" "df with columns customer_id, tenure_months, churn (0/1); 8.000 rows" Task "do a model" "fit a logistic regression predicting churn, with a stratified 80/20 split" Constraint — "use scikit-learn only; no additional installs; set random_state=42" Output — "return a function train_model(df) -> (model, metrics_dict) plus the ROC curve"

A prompt that works

I have a pandas DataFrame `df` with columns: customer_id, tenure_months, monthly_charges,
contract_type (categorical), churn (0/1). 8,000 rows, ~26% churn.

Write a scikit-learn pipeline that:
1. one-hot encodes contract_type and scales the numeric columns,
2. fits a logistic regression predicting churn,
3. evaluates it with stratified 5-fold cross-validation, reporting ROC-AUC and recall,
4. returns the fitted pipeline and a dict of metrics.

Use random_state=42. Do the encoding inside the pipeline, not before the split.
Explain in two lines why that last point matters.

The final instruction — explain why — is what turns the assistant from a code vending machine into a tutor. Use it constantly.

docs.title: 3. Verify before you trust
docs.text:
Generated code usually runs. Running is not the same as being correct. Before you keep any block:

  • Read it line by line. If you cannot say what a line does, ask the assistant to explain it.
  • Check the shapes. df.shape, y.value_counts(), X_train.shape — after every transformation.
  • Look for leakage. Was anything fitted (scaler, encoder, imputer, feature selection) before the train/test split, or using the target?
  • Sanity-check the metric. 99% accuracy on an imbalanced problem usually means the model predicts the majority class. Check recall, a confusion matrix, or a baseline.
  • Verify the API exists. Assistants occasionally invent function arguments. If an argument looks unfamiliar, check the library documentation.
  • Re-run from a clean kernel. "Restart and run all" — if the notebook does not reproduce, it is not finished.

docs.title: Failure modes we will see in this course
docs.text: Failure mode What it looks like How to catch it Data leakage Suspiciously high test score Check what was fitted before the split Wrong metric Great accuracy, useless model Look at the confusion matrix and the business cost of each error Fabricated API TypeError: unexpected keyword argument Check the library docs Silent type coercion Numbers become strings; means look wrong df.dtypes after every load and merge Plausible nonsense A confident explanation that is simply wrong Ask for the source; test the claim on a small example Hidden randomness Different results on each run Set random_state everywhere

docs.title: 4. What to delegate — and what not to
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["A task in your project"] --> B{"Is it mechanical?<br/>(syntax, plots, refactoring,<br/>boilerplate)"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Delegate it.<br/>Then review it."]
    B -->|No| D{"Is it a judgement call?<br/>(which metric, which features,<br/>what counts as success)"}
    D -->|Yes| E["Decide yourself.<br/>Use the assistant as a sounding board."]
    D -->|No| F["Ask it to teach you,<br/>then do it yourself."]

Delegate: syntax you have written a hundred times, plotting, docstrings, refactoring, translating an idea into library calls, and explaining an error message.

Do not delegate: choosing the target variable, deciding what counts as a good result, judging whether a feature would be available at prediction time, or interpreting what a result means for the business. Those are the parts you are being graded on.

docs.title: 5. Course policy
docs.text:
Allowed, expected, and disclosed

  1. Using an assistant is permitted and encouraged in homework and in the project.
  2. You must be able to explain every line you submit. Project presentations include questions about your own code. Code you cannot explain is treated as code you did not write.
  3. You must disclose your use in the assistant log of each delivery (next section).
  4. Never paste confidential or personal data into a public assistant. Use synthetic or public data in this course.

docs.title: The assistant log (required in both deliveries)
docs.text:
Half a page, at the end of the report. One row per meaningful use:

Task Tool What it produced What I changed or rejected Build the preprocessing pipeline Claude Full ColumnTransformer Moved the imputer inside the pipeline — it was leaking Plot ROC curves Copilot Plot function Kept as-is Explain class weights ChatGPT Explanation + example Used the idea, rewrote the code myself

A log that says "we used it for everything and changed nothing" is a weak log: it means nobody reviewed the work. A log with rejections in it is a strong one.

📈 Why this is graded. In a data team, the person who cannot defend their model does not get to deploy it. This course grades the same thing: your judgement about the code, not your speed at producing it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every term the course uses, in plain words, with the session where it first appears. When a term has a usual name in econometrics, it is given too.

docs.title: Data and evaluation
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Unit of analysis What one row represents (here, one household). Make it the unit you will make decisions about. 2 Nominal / ordinal variable Categories without order (region) / with an order but no fixed spacing (education level). 1 Target (label, outcome) The variable the model predicts: \(y\) in econometrics. 3 Feature (predictor) A variable the model uses as input: a regressor in econometrics. 3 Training set / test set The rows the model learns from / the rows kept aside to measure performance on unseen data. 3 Baseline The simplest possible prediction (the mean, or the majority class). Every model must beat it. 4 RMSE Root mean squared error: the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of the target. 3 Overfitting / underfitting Learning the noise of the training data (low train error, high test error) / being too rigid to learn the pattern. 3 Bias–variance trade-off Flexible models have low bias and high variance; rigid ones the reverse. The best test error is in between. 3 Hyperparameter A setting chosen before fitting (k in KNN, depth of a tree, the penalty λ), not learned from the data. 3 Cross-validation (k-fold) Split the training set into k folds; each fold takes a turn as validation. Gives a mean score and its spread. 4 Data leakage Information that would not be available at prediction time reaching the model. Makes scores look better than reality. 4 Target leakage A feature computed from the target (e.g. income_decile when predicting income). The predictive cousin of a bad control. 4 Proxy means test Predicting a household's welfare from easy-to-observe characteristics, to target social programmes. The course case. Case

docs.title: Preprocessing and pipelines
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Scaling (standardisation) Rescaling each variable to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so units do not decide distances or penalties. 4 Pipeline One object that chains preprocessing steps and a model, and fits them in the right order on each training fold. 4 Imputation Filling missing values. The rule depends on what missing means: unknown (median) or not applicable (0 / own category). 5 One-hot encoding Turning a categorical variable into one 0/1 column per category: dummy variables in econometrics. 5 ColumnTransformer Applies a different preprocessing pipeline to each group of columns. 5 Stratified split A split that keeps the same share of each class in every part. 5

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Logistic regression (logit) Models \(P(y = 1)\) as \(1/(1 + e^{-z})\) with \(z\) a linear score. The same model as in econometrics, judged by prediction. 5 Decision threshold The probability above which we predict "yes". 0.5 is a default, not a rule; it should follow from the cost of each error. 5 Confusion matrix The 2×2 table of true/false positives and negatives. 5 False positive / false negative Predicting "poor" for a non-poor household (inclusion error) / missing a poor household (exclusion error). 5 Accuracy Share of correct predictions. Misleading when one class is much more common. 5 Recall (sensitivity) Of the actual positives, the share the model finds: TP / (TP + FN). 5 Precision Of the predicted positives, the share that are right: TP / (TP + FP). 5 ROC curve Recall against false positive rate, for every threshold. 5 AUC Area under the ROC curve: the probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative. 0.5 = coin, 1 = perfect. 5 Odds ratio \(e^{\beta}\): how a one-unit change multiplies the odds. In a predictive model, an association, not a causal effect. 5

docs.title: Trees and ensembles
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Decision tree A sequence of yes/no questions ("does the head work more than 27.5 hours?") that ends in a prediction at each leaf. 6 Gini impurity How mixed a node is: \(1 - \sum_k p_k^2\). 0 if all households in it share the same class; 0.5 at a 50/50 mix. 6 Split The question that divides a node in two; the tree picks the one that lowers impurity the most. 6 Depth / min_samples_leaf How many questions in a row a tree may ask / the smallest group a leaf may contain. Both control overfitting. 6 Bootstrap / bagging Resampling the rows with replacement / training many models on bootstrap samples and averaging them, to cut variance. 6 Random forest Bagging of trees where each split only considers a random subset of features (max_features), so the trees disagree more and the average is better. 6 Out-of-bag (OOB) score Each tree is evaluated on the rows its bootstrap left out: a free validation score. 6 Gradient boosting Trees built one after another, each correcting the errors of the ones before; learning_rate sets how big each correction is. 6 Permutation importance How much the validation score drops when one feature is shuffled. Measures predictive use, not causal effect. 6

docs.title: Selection and shrinkage
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Forward (stepwise) selection Start with no variables and add, one at a time, the one that improves the CV score most. 7 Regularisation (penalisation) Adding a cost for large coefficients to the fitting criterion, trading a little bias for less variance. 7 Ridge (L2) Penalty \(\lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2\): shrinks all coefficients towards zero, never exactly to zero. 7 LASSO (L1) Penalty \(\lambda \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert\): shrinks, and sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it also selects variables. 7 Elastic Net A mix of the L1 and L2 penalties (l1_ratio). 7 λ and C The penalty strength. scikit-learn uses \(C = 1/\lambda\): a small C means a strong penalty. 7 Regularisation path How each coefficient changes as the penalty goes from strong to weak. 7 1-SE rule Choose the simplest model whose CV score is within one standard error of the best (SE = standard deviation across folds / √k). 7

docs.title: Unlabeled data
docs.text: Term Meaning Session Unsupervised learning Finding structure in the features when there is no target to predict. 8 Principal component (PC) A new axis, a weighted mix of the standardised variables, pointing where the data spread most. PC1 keeps the most variance, PC2 the most of what is left, and so on. 8 Explained variance ratio Share of the total variance a component keeps. Tells you how much a 2-D map hides. 8 Loadings The weights of each original variable in a component: what the axis "means". 8 k-means Splits the data into k groups by alternating two steps: assign each point to the nearest centroid, move each centroid to the mean of its points. 8 Centroid The average profile of a cluster. 8 Inertia Sum of squared distances from each point to its centroid. Always falls as k grows. 8 Local minimum (n_init) k-means can get stuck in a worse solution depending on its start. Several starts (n_init) keep the best. 8 Elbow / silhouette Two imperfect guides for k: where inertia stops falling fast / how much closer points are to their own cluster than to the next. 8 Hierarchical clustering Merges the closest households or groups step by step; the dendrogram shows every level at once. 8 Cluster profiling Describing each cluster in the original units, and only then looking at outcomes such as poverty. 8

docs.title: Program
docs.text: 5 ECTS Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María Compulsory · GEME track

docs.title: 1. Course identification
docs.text: Item Detail Course title Machine Learning — Business Applications Programme EGEI · Track GEME (Globalisation and Emerging Market Economies) ECTS 5 Prerequisites Applied Econometrics I and II Lecturer Sebastián Azócar M., MSc in Data Science Contact hizocar@gmail.com Language English Schedule Fridays, 13:00 – 16:00 · 11 September – 27 November 2026 (10 meetings) Tools Python · scikit-learn · an AI coding assistant of your choice Course case Targeting poor households with CASEN 2022

docs.title: 2. Course description
docs.text:
Machine learning (ML) uses algorithms that learn patterns from data instead of following rules written by hand. This course covers the statistical methods and techniques used in ML to make predictions with business applications: what a model can and cannot learn from data, how to evaluate it honestly, and how to turn a prediction into a decision someone can act on.

What changes this year. Code assistants have moved from novelty to standard equipment on a data team. Producing code is cheap now; being accountable for it is not. The course therefore runs two threads in parallel:

  • the modelling thread — the statistics and algorithms, which do not change because a machine writes the syntax for you; and
  • the workflow thread — using an assistant to scaffold, refactor, debug and explain code, and verifying its output with the same scepticism you would apply to a colleague's pull request.

The second thread is not a bonus topic: an assistant that produces a plausible-looking model with a silent data leak is worse than no assistant at all. Learning to catch that is part of the course.

docs.title: 3. Learning outcomes
docs.text:
On completion, students will be able to:

  1. Frame a business question as a supervised or unsupervised learning problem, and state what a good answer would look like.
  2. Prepare and explore real data in Python, reproducibly.
  3. Fit and tune regression and classification models, and justify the choice of method.
  4. Evaluate models honestly: train/test discipline, cross-validation, the bias–variance trade-off and the right metric for the business problem.
  5. Reduce and segment data without labels using principal components and clustering.
  6. Work with an AI coding assistant productively: prompt it precisely, review its output, test it, and identify when it is wrong.
  7. Communicate results, assumptions and limitations to a non-technical audience.

docs.title: 4. Learning methods and schedule
docs.text: Learning by doing. Sessions last three hours and follow the same rhythm: a concept block, a hands-on lab paired with your assistant, and applied or project work. Students are expected to read the assigned material before class, and a study load of at least three hours per week outside the classroom is assumed. All assessed work is project-based.

docs.title: Choosing the problem
docs.text:
Your question must name who decides what with your prediction: a ministry that targets a subsidy, a bank that approves a loan, a firm that tries to keep a customer. Two routes:

  • Your own dataset. Public data is fine (Kaggle, UCI, the World Bank, open government data, the Banco Central de Chile…), but the question must be yours. At least ~1,000 rows and a clear target.
  • CASEN, with another target. The course data has more questions in it than poverty: labour informality, public vs. private health insurance, overcrowding. Poverty and income are not allowed as targets, since we solve those in class.

Either way, write down early which variables you would really have at prediction time. Most project disasters start there.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: an honest first model
docs.text:
Checkpoint 1 · 40% of the final grade

Goal: a framed problem, a clean dataset and a first model whose error you can defend.

Instructions

  1. Frame the problem. The question, the target, the decision that changes, and the cost of each kind of mistake.
  2. Prepare the data. One row per unit of analysis. Document every row you drop and every variable you transform, and what missing means for each column with missing values.
  3. Split first; baseline next. A trivial model (the mean, or the majority class) that every later result is measured against.
  4. Build a pipeline. Preprocessing inside a Pipeline, with linear or logistic regression and at least one KNN model, chosen by cross-validation.
  5. Evaluate with the right metric. For classification, a confusion matrix and a threshold you justify with the costs from step 1.
  6. Leakage check. One paragraph: which features did you remove or keep, and why each one would be available at prediction time.
  7. Assistant log (see Code Assistants).

Grading rubric

Criterion Weight Framing: the question, the target, the decision and the cost of each mistake 20% Data preparation, with documented choices (including missing values) 20% Pipeline and validation: split, baseline, CV, no leakage 30% Metric and threshold, read honestly 20% Clarity of the memo and the assistant log 10%

docs.title: Final delivery: compare, decide, defend
docs.text:
Final delivery · 60% of the final grade

Goal: take the Checkpoint 1 project to a recommendation, using the full toolbox of the course and the feedback you received.

Instructions

  1. Respond to the feedback on Checkpoint 1: what you changed, and why.
  2. Apply at least three families of methods: your Checkpoint 1 model, a tree-based ensemble (Session 6), and either shrinkage (Session 7) or an unsupervised step (Session 8).
  3. Compare them honestly with cross-validation on the same splits, and explain the trade-offs: not only which one scored highest, but which one you would deploy and why.
  4. Interpret and recommend. What should the decision-maker do differently because of this model? Quantify the expected effect, with explicit assumptions.
  5. State the limitations, including what would break in production and what data you would need next.
  6. Assistant log.

Grading rubric

Criterion Weight Response to feedback and quality of the final pipeline 15% Breadth and correctness of the methods applied 25% Honest comparison and model choice 20% Recommendation, quantified and with limitations 20% Presentation and defence of your own code 20%

A model you cannot explain is not a finished project

The final presentation includes questions about your own code and the choices behind it. The assistant can write the pipeline, but only you can justify it.

docs.title: 1. A model is a rule learned from examples
docs.text:
A model takes inputs X and produces a prediction ŷ. Fitting means choosing the rule's parameters so that the predictions are as close as possible to the observed y — where "close" is defined by a cost function (for regression, typically the mean squared error).

Nothing in that sentence guarantees the rule will work on data it has never seen. That is the whole problem of the course.

docs.title: 2. KNN: the simplest useful predictor
docs.text:
K-nearest neighbours predicts a new case by looking at the k most similar cases in the training data and averaging (or voting on) their outcomes. It has no equation to interpret, which makes it a clean way to see the effect of one hyperparameter:

k Behaviour Consequence 1 Follows every point exactly Memorises noise — overfitting moderate Smooths locally Usually the sweet spot very large Predicts close to the global average Ignores structure — underfitting

docs.title: 3. Overfitting, underfitting and the bias–variance trade-off
docs.text:
• Underfitting (high bias): the model is too rigid to capture the pattern. Training error is high and test error is high.
  • Overfitting (high variance): the model captures the noise as if it were signal. Training error is very low and test error is high.

The polynomial regression lab makes this visible: as the degree grows, the fitted curve bends to touch every point, training error falls towards zero — and test error turns upwards.

💡 The rule to remember: a model that fits the training data perfectly has told you nothing. The only number that carries information is the error on data the model has not seen.

docs.title: 4. Training error vs. test error
docs.text: We split the data before fitting, and we report the test error. Today this is a simple hold-out split; in Session 4 we replace it with cross-validation and go hunting for the ways this discipline quietly breaks.

docs.title: 🧪 Lab: from underfitting to overfitting
docs.text:
In the Session 3 notebook, fit polynomials of increasing degree to the same data and plot training and test error against the degree. Identify the degree at which test error stops improving.

Use the assistant as a tutor

Explain, in five lines and without formulas, why the training error of a polynomial regression
keeps falling as the degree increases while the test error eventually rises.
Then give me the scikit-learn code to reproduce that with a train/test split, and plot both
curves against the polynomial degree.
Finally: name two things about this plot that could mislead me.
The last line is the one that matters. An assistant that is asked for the weaknesses of its own output is far more useful than one asked only for code.

Verify before keeping: was the split made before fitting? Is the same scaling applied to both sets? Is random_state fixed so the plot is reproducible?

docs.title: ❓ Today's question
docs.text: Last session we predicted household income from a few observable characteristics. How do we know the error we report is the error we would get on households the model has never seen?

docs.title: 🔁 What you already know

docs.title: ✨ New today
docs.text: Tool What it is for StandardScaler Put variables on the same scale so that distances (KNN) are fair Pipeline / make_pipeline Glue preprocessing and model into one object, fitted in the right order KFold + cross_val_score Choose hyperparameters (k) without touching the test set Data leakage Three ways information from the answer sneaks into the model

docs.title: 🗓️ Agenda (3 hours)
docs.text: Time Block 13:00 – 13:15 Recap of Session 3: train vs. test error, KNN, bias–variance 13:15 – 14:10 Scaling, by hand and in code · the Pipeline 14:10 – 14:25 Break 14:25 – 15:05 Cross-validation: choosing k without touching the test set 15:05 – 16:00 Leakage hunt on the case data · assistant audit

docs.title: 1. The setup
docs.text:
We predict log income per capita from three observables: age of the head of household, years of schooling and household size. The log is there because income is extremely skewed. The first number every model must beat is the baseline: predicting the average for everyone.

Model Test RMSE (log income) Baseline: everybody gets the mean 0.707 Linear regression 0.610 KNN, k = 1 0.820 (train: 0.659) KNN, k = 100, scaled 0.582

Move the slider. To draw it in two dimensions, the figure uses one variable (years of schooling) and 400 households, so its best k and its errors differ from the three-variable table above. The shape of the story is the same: with k = 1 the curve chases every household and the test error jumps, and with a very large k it flattens into the average.

docs.title: 2. Scaling, and why order matters
docs.text:
KNN measures distance. Age ranges from 15 to 100, schooling from 0 to 25, so without scaling the variable with the widest range dominates just because of its units. StandardScaler fixes that, but it learns a mean and a standard deviation, and anything learned must come from the training set only.

Worked example by hand: scaling changes who your neighbours are

We want to predict log income per capita for a new household: head aged 40, 12 years of schooling, 4 members. Four training households, and k = 2:

Age Schooling Size log income p.c. A 40 17 4 13.5 B 49 12 4 12.8 C 41 6 4 12.2 D 55 12 3 12.9

Without scaling (plain Euclidean distance): A = √(0² + 5² + 0²) = 5.0 · B = √(9²) = 9.0 · C = √(1² + 6²) = 6.1 · D = √(15² + 1²) = 15.0. The two nearest are A and C, so the prediction is (13.5 + 12.2) / 2 = 12.85, about CLP 381,000 per person.

With scaling (divide each difference by the standard deviation in the training data: 16.5 for age, 4.5 for schooling, 1.5 for size): A = 5/4.5 = 1.11 · B = 9/16.5 = 0.55 · C = √(0.06² + 1.33²) = 1.34 · D = √(0.91² + 0.67²) = 1.13. Now the two nearest are B and A, and the prediction is (12.8 + 13.5) / 2 = 13.15, about CLP 514,000.

Same data, same k, a 35% different prediction. Without scaling, nine years of age "looked" bigger than six years of schooling, purely because of the units.

The standard deviations you divide by are learned from data. That is where the order of operations starts to matter:

docs.title: 3. The pipeline
docs.text:
A Pipeline makes the right order automatic: .fit() fits the scaler and then the model on the data it receives, and .predict() applies both.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=100))
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: 4. Cross-validation: choosing k without peeking
docs.text:
If we try twenty values of k and keep the best test score, the test set has chosen the model and its score is no longer honest. Instead we split the training set into 5 folds. Each fold takes a turn as validation while the other four fit the pipeline, and the scaler is refitted every time.

What CV gives you Our case (k = 100) Mean error — the expected performance 0.572 Spread across folds — how much is luck ± 0.005 A fold that collapses — something structural none here

From econometrics to ML

  • In econometrics you judge a model in sample (R², t-statistics). Here the only score that counts is computed out of sample, on households the model never saw.
  • Adding a regressor never lowers the in-sample R². It can easily raise the test error. That is overfitting, the bias–variance trade-off of Session 3.
  • The spread of the CV scores plays a role similar to a standard error: it tells you how much your number would move with a different sample.
  • Target leakage is the predictive cousin of a bad control: a regressor that is itself a function of the outcome. In both cases the model looks better and answers the wrong question.

docs.title: 5. The leakage hunt
docs.text:
Leakage is any way information you would not have at prediction time reaches the model. Toggle the variables and watch the error:

Leak On our data Lesson Scaling before the split 0.582 → 0.582: negligible with 15,000 rows Keep the habit anyway: with small data, or with steps that learn more (imputers, target encoders, feature selection), the same mistake inflates scores A feature built from the target (income_decile) 0.582 → 0.313 The decile is computed from income. In a proxy means test you would never have it Choosing the model on the test set Optimistic by construction Choose with CV, test once at the end The same unit on both sides Avoided: one row per household With one row per person, relatives would sit in train and test

⚠️ The rule of thumb: if a result is much better than you expected, do not celebrate. Ask of every feature: would I have this value at the moment I need the prediction?

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts How to avoid it Fitting the scaler (or imputer) on the full data Test information shapes the training data; scores become optimistic Put every learned step inside a Pipeline Choosing k (or anything) by looking at the test score The test score becomes the best of many tries Choose with cross_val_score on the training set; test once Reporting only the mean CV score Hides whether the result is stable or lucky Report mean ± spread across folds Forgetting the baseline "RMSE 0.58" means nothing on its own Always show the predict-the-mean error next to it Using variables you would not have at prediction time The model is useless in production, however good it looks For every feature, ask when you would know its value Splitting people when the decision is about households Relatives on both sides leak shared information Make the row the unit you predict for, or use GroupKFold

docs.title: ✅ Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. Why is it wrong to try k = 1, 5, 25, 100 and keep the one with the lowest test RMSE?

Because the test set has then chosen the model. Its score is the best of four tries, so it is optimistic, and you no longer have untouched data to report an honest error. Choose k with cross-validation on the training set and use the test set once, at the end.

2. The five fold RMSEs for k = 100 are 0.574, 0.577, 0.577, 0.570 and 0.563. What do you report?

Mean = (0.574 + 0.577 + 0.577 + 0.570 + 0.563) / 5 = 0.572, with a spread of about ±0.005. The folds agree to within a few thousandths, so the result is stable. Compare it with the baseline of 0.707: the model cuts the error by about 19%.

3. A classmate predicts income with R² = 0.95 using schooling, household size and income_decile. What is your first question?

Would you know income_decile before knowing income? No: the decile is computed from income. The feature leaks the target. Without it the honest error is around 0.58, not 0.31.

4. Is df['head_weekly_hours'].fillna(0) before the split a leak? And filling with the mean?

Filling with 0 is a fixed rule that does not look at the data, so it cannot leak, and it is also the correct value (missing means the head does not work). Filling with the mean learns a number from the data. Done before the split, the test rows would help compute it. Learned steps go inside the pipeline.

5. Scaling before the split barely changed our RMSE (0.582 vs 0.582). So why bother?

Because with 15,000 rows a mean and a standard deviation hardly move when you add the test rows. With a few hundred rows, or with steps that learn much more from the data (target encoding, feature selection, imputing with a model), the same mistake can inflate scores a lot. The pipeline makes the right order automatic, so you never have to judge case by case.

docs.title: 🧪 Lab
docs.text:
Work through the notebook in pairs. It rebuilds every number on this page from the raw CSV.

📓 Session 4 — The ML Pipeline ·

Assistant skill: audit a pipeline for leakage

Here is my scikit-learn code (paste it). Review it for data leakage.
For every transformation, say whether it is fitted before or after the train/test split.
For every feature, say whether it would be available at prediction time in a proxy means test.
List the problems first, then the corrected code.
Then check it against the notebook. Did it catch income_decile? Did it flag anything that is not actually a problem? Both kinds of mistake go in your assistant log.

Key takeaways

  • Split first. The test set stands for future households; nothing you decide may use it.
  • Scale for distance-based models. KNN compares households through distances, and units must not decide who is "near".
  • Anything learned goes inside the pipeline: scalers, imputers, encoders, the model.
  • Choose with cross-validation, report mean ± spread, test once.
  • Suspect great results. For every feature, ask whether you would have it at prediction time.
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=100))
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = -cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())
model.fit(X_train, y_train)          # refit on all training data, then test once

docs.title: ❓ Today's question
docs.text: A social programme does not pay "a predicted income". It decides yes or no. Can we predict directly whether a household is poor, and which mistakes should we be more afraid of?

docs.title: 🔁 What you already know
docs.text: From Session 4: split first, put preprocessing inside a Pipeline, choose with cross-validation, and suspect any feature you would not have at prediction time. From econometrics: the logit model.

docs.title: ✨ New today
docs.text: Tool What it is for LogisticRegression The logit, now judged by how well it predicts unseen households Confusion matrix · precision · recall Separate the two kinds of mistake The decision threshold Turn probabilities into decisions, according to the cost of each mistake ROC curve · AUC Judge the model across all thresholds stratify= · StratifiedKFold Keep the 23% of poor households in every split OneHotEncoder · SimpleImputer · ColumnTransformer Bring categorical variables and missing values inside the pipeline cross_val_predict Out-of-fold probabilities for choosing the threshold without the test set

docs.title: 🗓️ Agenda (3 hours)
docs.text: Time Block 13:00 – 13:15 Recap: the leakage hunt, and why income cannot be a feature 13:15 – 14:10 Logistic regression as a predictor · the accuracy trap · confusion matrix 14:10 – 14:25 Break 14:25 – 15:05 The threshold as a policy decision · ROC and AUC 15:05 – 15:35 Lab: categorical variables and missing values in the pipeline 15:35 – 16:00 Project launch: groups, question, data

docs.title: 1. The same model you know, used to predict
docs.text:
In econometrics you used the logit to estimate effects. The equation is identical:

\[P(\text{poor} \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p)}}\]

What changes is the question: not "is \(\beta_1\) significant?" but "how well does this predict households the model has never seen?". Here is the logit with just one variable, years of schooling. Move the coefficients, then let maximum likelihood find them.

Worked example by hand: from a score to a probability

The fitted one-variable model is \(z = -0.352 - 0.086 \times \text{schooling}\), and \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) (coefficients rounded to three decimals, so the notebook may differ in the third decimal).

Schooling \(z\) \(e^{-z}\) \(p = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) 8 years −0.352 − 0.688 = −1.040 2.829 1 / 3.829 = 0.261 12 years −0.352 − 1.032 = −1.384 3.991 1 / 4.991 = 0.200 16 years −0.352 − 1.376 = −1.728 5.629 1 / 6.629 = 0.151

Each extra year multiplies the odds of being poor by \(e^{-0.086} = 0.918\), so four more years multiply them by 0.709. Notice that no household gets a probability above 0.5 in this model. With a 0.5 threshold, schooling alone would never select anyone.

From econometrics to ML

  • Same model, different scorecard. In econometrics you ask whether \(\beta_1\) is significantly different from zero. Here you ask how well the model ranks and classifies unseen households.
  • Significant ≠ useful for prediction. With 15,000 rows almost any variable is significant, even when adding it does not move the test AUC. The reverse also happens.
  • Pseudo-R² ↔ AUC and the confusion matrix. They summarise different things: fit of the likelihood vs. ability to separate classes at the thresholds you would actually use.
  • Odds ratios are associations. In a predictive model the coefficients absorb everything correlated with them. Do not read them as causal effects of schooling or region.

docs.title: 2. The accuracy trap
docs.text:
About 23% of households are poor, so a "model" that says nobody is poor is already 76.9% accurate. Our logistic regression with all observable variables reaches 79.7%. That looks like a small win, and it hides a disaster:

predicted not poor predicted poor actually not poor 2,754 130 actually poor 633 233

At the default threshold of 0.5 the model misses almost three out of four poor households (recall = 0.27).

  • Recall: of the poor households, the share we reach. TP / (TP + FN)
  • Precision: of the households we select, the share that are actually poor. TP / (TP + FP)

docs.title: 3. The threshold is a policy decision
docs.text:
.predict() says "poor" when the probability is above 0.5, but nothing makes 0.5 right. Lower it and the programme reaches more poor households (recall ↑) while subsidising more households that are not poor (precision ↓). How much each mistake costs is not a statistical question. It belongs to whoever runs the programme. Your job is to make the trade-off visible.

Threshold Poor reached Poor missed Non-poor subsidised Recall Precision 0.50 233 633 130 0.27 0.64 0.30 528 338 538 0.61 0.50 0.20 684 182 1,016 0.79 0.40

Worked example by hand: what does each threshold cost?

Say that excluding a poor household costs 3 units and subsidising a non-poor household costs 1. Using the table above:

  • Threshold 0.50: 3 × 633 + 1 × 130 = 2,029
  • Threshold 0.20: 3 × 182 + 1 × 1,016 = 1,562

Lowering the threshold to 0.20 roughly multiplies the false positives by eight, and the total cost still falls by almost a quarter, because each missed poor household weighs three times as much. The widget finds the cheapest threshold for any pair of costs (≈ 0.24 for 3:1, total 1,482).

The ROC curve shows every threshold at once, and the AUC summarises it: the probability that a random poor household gets a higher score than a random non-poor one. Ours is 0.79, or 0.78 ± 0.01 with stratified 5-fold cross-validation.

docs.title: 4. All the information, inside the pipeline
docs.text:
Most of what we know about a household is categorical, and some values are missing. What missing means decides the rule:

Column Why it is missing Rule inside the pipeline head_weekly_hours the head does not work (6,105 cases) fill with 0, not the median (which would invent a 45-hour week) head_weekly_hours an employed head did not know (87 cases) same column, different meaning: 0 is wrong here (notebook exercise 4) head_job_type the head does not work its own category, "missing" schooling, insurance, overcrowding "doesn't know" (rare) median, or its own category 
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num",   make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), NUM),
    ("hours", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=0), StandardScaler()), HOURS),
    ("cat",   make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing"),
                            OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")), CAT),
])
model = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000))])

This is the Session 4 pipeline with more steps. Every learned value (medians, categories, scales) is still learned on training folds only.

docs.title: 5. The leak, again
docs.text: Add income_per_capita and the AUC jumps from 0.79 to 0.965. Poverty is defined by comparing income per capita with a poverty line, so this model only rediscovers the definition, and needs the one variable a proxy means test exists to avoid.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts How to avoid it Reporting accuracy on an imbalanced problem 77% is achievable by selecting nobody Show the confusion matrix, recall and precision next to the baseline Leaving the threshold at 0.5 0.5 encodes "both errors cost the same", a policy choice nobody made Choose the threshold from the costs of each error Choosing the threshold on the test set The test score becomes optimistic (Leak C again) Use cross-validated predictions on the training set Imputing "not applicable" values with the median Invents a 45-hour week for people who do not work Ask what missing means; use 0 or a "missing" category One-hot encoding before the split Categories seen only in test leak into training Encode inside the ColumnTransformer with handle_unknown="ignore" Splitting without stratify Train and test can end up with different shares of poor households train_test_split(..., stratify=y) and StratifiedKFold

docs.title: ✅ Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. A model has 85% accuracy on a problem where 85% of cases are negative. Is it good?

You cannot tell from accuracy. "Predict negative for everyone" also scores 85%. Look at the confusion matrix: how many positives does it find (recall), and how many of its positives are right (precision)?

2. From the matrix at 0.5 (TP = 233, FN = 633, FP = 130, TN = 2,754), compute recall and precision.

Recall = 233 / (233 + 633) = 233 / 866 = 0.269: the model reaches about one poor household in four. Precision = 233 / (233 + 130) = 233 / 363 = 0.642: of those it selects, about six in ten are poor.

3. The ministry says: 'we prefer to subsidise some non-poor households rather than miss poor ones'. Do you raise or lower the threshold?

Lower it. A lower threshold selects more households, so recall rises and precision falls. That is exactly the trade the ministry is willing to make. The cost ratio tells you how far to go.

4. Our AUC is 0.79. Explain it to a policymaker in one sentence.

"If you pick one poor and one non-poor household at random, the model gives the poor one a higher score 79% of the time." (A coin would do it 50% of the time.)

5. Adding income per capita raises the AUC to 0.965. Why should we still not use it?

Poverty is defined by comparing income per capita with a poverty line, so the model just rediscovers the definition. The point of a proxy means test is that income is not reliably observed when the decision is made. A feature you will not have at prediction time is a leak, however good it makes the score look.

docs.title: 🧪 Lab
docs.text:
📓 Session 5 — Classification ·

Assistant skill: choose the metric, don't accept the default

I have a logistic regression that predicts whether a household is poor (23% positive class).
Here is my confusion matrix at threshold 0.5: (paste). Explain in plain language what each cell
means for a social programme. Then write code that picks the threshold minimising 3*FN + 1*FP on
cross-validated predictions (not on the test set). Tell me why that last condition matters.
Check that it uses cross_val_predict (or equivalent) on the training set. An assistant that tunes the threshold on the test set has just reintroduced Leak C from Session 4.

Key takeaways

  • Accuracy can hide a disaster. Always compare with the majority-class baseline and look at the confusion matrix.
  • Recall and precision answer different policy questions: whom do we reach, and whom do we pay by mistake?
  • The threshold is a decision, not a default. It follows from the cost of each error. Choose it with cross-validated predictions.
  • AUC judges the ranking across all thresholds. It is useful for comparing models, not for choosing a cut-off.
  • What missing means decides how to fill it, and every learned step stays inside the pipeline.
model = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000))])
p = cross_val_predict(model, X_train, y_train, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42),
                      method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
best_t = min(np.linspace(0.05, 0.9, 86),
             key=lambda t: 3 * ((p < t) & (y_train == 1)).sum() + ((p >= t) & (y_train == 0)).sum())
# best_t ≈ 0.26, chosen without ever looking at the test set

docs.title: 1. A tree is a sequence of questions
docs.text:
Imagine a social worker with a clipboard. The first question splits the households into two piles; each pile gets its own next question, and so on. After a few questions, each final pile (a leaf) is a group of similar households, and the model predicts the share of poor households in that pile.

The tree learns which questions to ask. To do that it needs a way to say how good a pile is.

docs.title: 2. Choosing a question: the Gini impurity
docs.text:
A group with a share \(p\) of poor households has Gini impurity

\[G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1-p)\]

In words: pick two households at random from the group. \(G\) is the probability that one is poor and the other is not. A pure group (all poor, or none) has \(G = 0\); a 50/50 group has the maximum, \(G = 0.5\). A split is scored by the weighted average impurity of the two groups it creates, and the tree keeps the split with the lowest score.

Worked example by hand

Eight households, three of them poor:

Household Years of schooling Household size Poor H1 6 5 ✔ H2 8 3 ✔ H3 8 2 H4 10 6 ✔ H5 12 3 H6 12 1 H7 14 4 H8 16 2

Before any split: \(p = 3/8 = 0.375\), so \(G = 2 \times 0.375 \times 0.625 = 0.469\).

Split A, "schooling ≤ 10?" - Yes group: H1–H4, 3 poor out of 4, so \(G = 2 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.375\). - No group: H5–H8, 0 poor out of 4, so \(G = 0\). - Weighted: \(\tfrac{4}{8} \times 0.375 + \tfrac{4}{8} \times 0 = 0.188\).

Split B, "household size ≤ 3?" - Yes group: H2, H3, H5, H6, H8, 1 poor out of 5, so \(G = 2 \times 0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.320\). - No group: H1, H4, H7, 2 poor out of 3, so \(G = 2 \times \tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{1}{3} = 0.444\). - Weighted: \(\tfrac{5}{8} \times 0.320 + \tfrac{3}{8} \times 0.444 = 0.367\).

Split A removes \(0.469 - 0.188 = 0.281\) of impurity and split B only \(0.102\), so the tree asks about schooling first. A real tree does this for every variable and every possible cut, then repeats inside each group.

Now try it on the 11,250 training households. On real data no single variable separates poor from non-poor cleanly. The best cut on schooling (≤ 12) only takes the impurity from 0.355 to 0.346.

Notice what the tree does not need: scaling. "Schooling ≤ 12" is the same question in years or in standard deviations. Categories still need one-hot encoding, because scikit-learn's trees split on numbers.

docs.title: 3. The tree we actually get
docs.text: Fitted on all the variables, the first question is "does the head work 27.5 hours a week or less?", a group that includes heads who do not work at all. On the yes side 33% of households are poor; on the no side, 13%. The next questions differ by branch: for low-hours households the tree asks about the head's age, then about housing tenure or household size; for full-time workers it asks whether there are children, then about the type of job or schooling. That is an interaction, found without anyone writing it down.

docs.title: 4. How deep? Overfitting, again
docs.text:
Every extra level doubles the number of groups. Deep enough, each leaf holds a handful of households and the tree memorises them: it is KNN with k = 1 all over again. Move the slider and watch both the curves and the tree.

Tree Train AUC CV AUC max_depth=3 0.738 0.735 max_depth=6 (best by CV) 0.795 0.759 max_depth=12 0.929 0.693 No limit 1.000 0.618 No depth limit, min_samples_leaf=100 — 0.763 Logit, for reference 0.789 0.781

Even the best single tree stays below the logit. A tree is flexible but unstable: change a few households and the first question can change, and everything below it with it.

docs.title: 5. Many trees: bagging and random forests
docs.text:
The cure for instability is to grow many trees and average them.

  1. Bootstrap: draw 11,250 households with replacement from the training set. Some appear twice, and about a third are left out.
  2. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): fit one deep tree per bootstrap sample and average their probabilities. Each tree overfits in its own way, and the average cancels much of that noise.
  3. Random forest: at each split, a tree may only consider a random subset of the variables (max_features, by default the square root of their number). The trees become more different from each other, so their average improves further.

The households a tree never saw are its out-of-bag sample: a free validation set.

Model CV AUC Bagging (all variables at each split) 0.787 ± 0.004 Random forest (300 trees, min_samples_leaf=5) 0.797 ± 0.007 Random forest, out-of-bag AUC (no CV needed) 0.798

docs.title: 6. Trees that learn from their mistakes: gradient boosting
docs.text:
A forest grows its trees independently and averages them. Boosting grows them in sequence: each new tree is small, and it is fitted to what the current model still gets wrong. It is added with a small weight (learning_rate), so the model improves step by step. Too many steps overfit, so HistGradientBoostingClassifier sets aside 10% of the training data and stops early when that held-out score stops improving.

From econometrics to ML

  • In a regression, an interaction exists only if you write hours × children into the model. A tree finds interactions and thresholds on its own. That is its strength, and also why it overfits.
  • A tree has no coefficients and no standard errors. You cannot ask "is schooling significant?". You can ask "how much worse does the model predict without schooling?" (section 8).
  • Bagging is the bootstrap you know from econometrics. There it estimated the variability of an estimator; here it reduces the variability of a prediction by averaging.
  • None of these models is causal. A tree that splits on hours of work is not saying that more hours would lift a household out of poverty.

docs.title: 7. The race, done properly
docs.text:
Four models, compared with the same 5 folds and the same test set. Each model gets its own threshold, chosen to minimise 3·FN + FP on out-of-fold probabilities (cross_val_predict) from the training set, never on the test set.

Model Train AUC CV AUC Test AUC Threshold Recall Precision Cost 3·FN + FP Logit (Session 5) 0.789 0.781 ± 0.009 0.794 0.26 0.680 0.454 1,540 Tree (depth 4) 0.757 0.746 ± 0.009 0.767 0.24 0.682 0.446 1,560 Random forest 0.903 0.797 ± 0.007 0.814 0.24 0.745 0.460 1,421 Gradient boosting 0.910 0.798 ± 0.007 0.815 0.20 0.788 0.439 1,422

The ensembles gain about 0.02 of AUC and cut the policy cost by about 8%. The forest reaches 75% of poor households against the logit's 68%, at slightly better precision; boosting picks a lower threshold and reaches 79%, at lower precision, for the same total cost. That gain is real, but it is not a revolution, and it comes at a price (section 9).

docs.title: 8. What does the forest rely on? Permutation importance
docs.text:
feature_importances_ (impurity importance) adds up how much each column reduced the Gini while the trees were being trained, and it favours variables with many possible cut points. Permutation importance asks a cleaner question on the test set: if I shuffle this column so it carries no information, how much AUC does the model lose?

Variable AUC lost when shuffled head_age 0.037 head_weekly_hours 0.031 has_children 0.029 housing_tenure 0.028 household_type 0.019 has_elderly 0.018

Two cautions. Importance describes what the model uses to predict, not what causes poverty. And when two variables carry the same information (years of schooling and education level), shuffling one costs little, because the other covers for it.

docs.title: 9. Accuracy vs. explanation
docs.text: A household excluded from a programme has the right to ask why. With a depth-3 or depth-4 tree the answer is a short chain of questions: "the head works more than 27.5 hours, there are no children, and the head is not self-employed". With 300 trees there is no short answer. Against the depth-4 tree, the forest gains about 0.05 of AUC and saves about 140 cost units on 3,750 test households. Whether that is worth the loss of transparency is a decision for the programme. Your job is to put both numbers on the table.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts How to avoid it Growing a tree with no limits Train AUC 1.000, CV AUC 0.618: pure memorisation Set max_depth or min_samples_leaf and choose them by CV Comparing models on different splits Differences can be luck of the split, not the model Same cv object and same test set for every model Reading feature_importances_ as causal effects Importance is about prediction, and impurity importance is biased Use permutation importance, and still don't read it causally Choosing each model's threshold on the test set The comparison becomes optimistic, the Leak C of Session 4 cross_val_predict on the training set Keeping the forest because its AUC is highest You lose the ability to explain each decision Report the trade-off and let the decision-maker weigh it Scaling features "just in case" before a tree Harmless but useless, and it adds a step you must explain Trees only need numbers, not comparable scales

docs.title: ✅ Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. A leaf holds 50 households, 10 of them poor. What is its Gini impurity, and what probability does the tree predict for a new household that lands there?

\(p = 10/50 = 0.2\), so \(G = 2 \times 0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.32\). The tree predicts the leaf's poverty share: a probability of 0.2. Whether that household gets the subsidy depends on the threshold (0.24 for the forest, 0.26 for the logit), not on the tree.

2. The unrestricted tree has a train AUC of 1.000 and a CV AUC of 0.618. Explain both numbers.

With no depth limit, the tree keeps splitting until each leaf is pure, often a single household, so it predicts every training household perfectly (AUC 1.000). Those leaves describe individual households, not patterns, so on households it has not seen the rules are mostly noise (CV AUC 0.618, much worse than the logit's 0.781). It is the same phenomenon as KNN with k = 1.

3. Why does a tree not need StandardScaler, while KNN does?

KNN compares households by distance, and distance depends on units. A tree only asks "is this value above or below a cut?", and the answer is the same in years, months or standard deviations. One-hot encoding is still needed, because scikit-learn's trees only split numeric columns.

4. Bagging scored 0.787 and the random forest 0.797. What does the forest do differently, and why does it help?

At each split, each tree of the forest may only look at a random subset of the variables. With bagging, every tree tends to start with the same strong question (hours of work), so the trees are similar and their errors are correlated. Averaging correlated errors cancels little. Forcing the trees to differ makes their errors less correlated, so the average cancels more noise.

5. The ministry insists that every excluded household can be told why. What do you recommend, and what does it cost?

A shallow tree (depth 3–4), presented as a scorecard. On our test set the depth-4 tree costs 1,560 against 1,421 for the random forest: about 140 more cost units, mainly poor households left out. One honest option is to use the forest to rank households and the tree to explain the rule, checking that the two rarely disagree, but that is a policy choice, not a statistical one. Put the numbers on the table.

Assistant skill: refactor a script into functions

Here is my notebook code that evaluates four classifiers (paste it).
Refactor it into two functions: cost_threshold(p, y, fn_cost, fp_cost) and
evaluate(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, cv) -> dict.

Then run the old and the new code and compare the results table number by number. A refactor that changes a result is a bug, even if the new number looks better. A common one: the assistant "simplifies" by choosing the threshold on X_test.

Key takeaways

forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, n_jobs=-1)

docs.text: Our poverty model asks 19 questions in every household visit. Each question costs interview time, can be shaded by an applicant who knows what the programme is looking for, and has to be verified. Which variables do we really need? docs.text: Tool What it is for The cost of many variables Variance, interpretability and, in policy, the cost of collecting each one Forward stepwise selection Build the model one variable at a time, keeping the one that raises CV AUC most (SequentialFeatureSelector is the scikit-learn version for matrix columns) Ridge (L2) · LASSO (L1) · Elastic Net Penalised regression: shrink coefficients instead of choosing them (l1_ratio = 0, 1, or in between) C = 1/λ The penalty strength in scikit-learn. Small C = strong penalty The regularisation path All the models from "no variables" to "all variables", as the penalty weakens The 1-SE rule Pick the simplest (most penalised) model whose CV AUC is within one standard error of the best, where SE = fold sd / √5

docs.title: 🗓️ Agenda (3 hours)
docs.text: Time Block 13:00 – 13:15 Recap of Session 6 · questions on Checkpoint 1 13:15 – 13:45 The cost of a variable · forward selection: how many questions does the form need? 13:45 – 14:10 Shrinkage: the penalty, the geometry, why LASSO gives exact zeros 14:10 – 14:25 Break 14:25 – 15:35 Lab: the LASSO path on the poverty model · when shrinkage pays off 15:35 – 16:00 Project work: which variables does your model need?

docs.title: 1. Why fewer variables?
docs.text:
More variables never hurt the fit on the training data. They can hurt in three other ways:

  • Variance. Every coefficient is estimated with noise. With few observations per coefficient the model starts fitting that noise, the overfitting of Session 3 in a new form.
  • Interpretability. A model with 7 inputs can be explained to a ministry. A model with 76 columns is a black box even if it is linear.
  • Cost and gaming. In a proxy means test each variable is a question someone must ask, record and verify. The more questions, the more expensive the visit, and the more chances for an applicant to give the answer that qualifies.

Two families of tools answer the question: selection (keep some variables, drop the rest) and shrinkage (keep all of them, but pull their coefficients towards zero).

docs.title: 2. Forward stepwise selection: build the form one question at a time
docs.text:
Trying every possible form would mean \(2^{19} \approx 524{,}000\) models. Forward stepwise selection is the greedy shortcut: start with no questions, and at each step add the one that raises the cross-validated AUC the most.

We select questions (raw variables), not dummy columns: a form cannot ask "is the region Maule?" without asking the region. Press Play and watch the gains flatten:

Questions Last question added CV AUC 1 head_job_type 0.657 2 head_age 0.702 3 head_education 0.726 5 has_children 0.757 7 region 0.771 8 head_weekly_hours 0.774 10 overcrowding 0.779 19 (all) 0.781

Eight questions get within 0.01 of the full form (0.774 vs 0.781). Seven reach 0.771, a hair below the line. The 0.01 is a convention, not a law, so show the whole curve and not just the cut-off. The order tells a story too. head_schooling_years only enters at step 18, because head_education already carries almost the same information. Greedy selection keeps one of two correlated variables and ignores the other, which makes the second one redundant, not irrelevant.

docs.title: 3. Shrinkage: a price on every coefficient
docs.text:
Selection is all-or-nothing. Shrinkage keeps every variable, but adds a price for large coefficients to the quantity the model minimises:

\[\underbrace{\text{log-loss}(\beta)}_{\text{fit the data}} \; + \; \lambda \cdot \underbrace{\text{penalty}(\beta)}_{\text{keep coefficients small}}\] Method Penalty What it does Ridge (L2) \(\sum_j \beta_j^2\) Shrinks all coefficients towards 0. None becomes exactly 0 LASSO (L1) \(\sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert\) Shrinks, and sets some coefficients exactly to 0, so it selects as well Elastic Net a mix of both Sparse like LASSO, more stable when variables are correlated

Read it in plain words: \(\lambda\) is the exchange rate between fit and simplicity. With \(\lambda = 0\) you get the ordinary logit. As \(\lambda\) grows, a coefficient has to "earn" its size by improving the fit enough to pay for it. scikit-learn uses the inverse, \(C = 1/\lambda\), so a small C means a strong penalty.

Because the penalty compares coefficients with each other, all variables must be on the same scale. A coefficient on income in pesos is tiny and a coefficient on a 0/1 dummy is large, for the same importance. That is why the StandardScaler stays inside the pipeline.

Worked example by hand

Take two standardised, uncorrelated variables whose unpenalised (OLS) coefficients are \(\hat\beta_1 = 0.80\) and \(\hat\beta_2 = 0.15\). In this simple case the penalised solutions have closed forms:

  • Ridge divides every coefficient by the same factor: \(\beta^{\text{ridge}} = \hat\beta / (1 + \lambda)\)
  • LASSO subtracts \(\lambda\) and stops at zero: \(\beta^{\text{lasso}} = \text{sign}(\hat\beta)\cdot\max(|\hat\beta| - \lambda,\; 0)\)

With \(\lambda = 0.2\):

\(\hat\beta\) (no penalty) Ridge: \(\hat\beta / 1.2\) LASSO: \(\max(\lvert\hat\beta\rvert - 0.2, 0)\) \(\beta_1\) 0.80 0.80 / 1.2 = 0.667 0.80 − 0.20 = 0.60 \(\beta_2\) 0.15 0.15 / 1.2 = 0.125 0.15 − 0.20 < 0 → 0

Ridge shrinks both coefficients by the same proportion. LASSO shrinks both by the same amount, and the small one does not survive. That is the whole mechanism of selection by LASSO: a coefficient smaller than \(\lambda\) is set to zero.

Why does the absolute value produce exact zeros and the square does not? A penalty is equivalent to a budget: the coefficients must stay inside a shape (a diamond for L1, a circle for L2), and the solution is the first point where the contours of the loss touch it. Switch between L1 and L2 and shrink the budget:

The diamond has corners on the axes, and the contours usually touch it at a corner, where one coefficient is exactly zero. The circle has no corners, so coefficients get smaller but never vanish.

docs.title: 4. The LASSO path on the poverty model
docs.text:
We fit the L1-penalised logit for 40 values of C, from C = 0.001 (almost every coefficient is zero) to C = 10 (almost no penalty), and record three things each time: the coefficients, the cross-validated AUC, and how many questions still have at least one non-zero coefficient.

Penalty choice C Coefficients ≠ 0 (of 76) Questions used (of 19) CV AUC (± SE) CV-best 0.943 60 18 0.781 ± 0.004 1-SE rule 0.070 35 18 0.777 ± 0.004

The 1-SE rule picks the simplest (most penalised) model whose CV AUC is within one standard error of the best, where SE = fold sd / √5. The fold standard deviation is 0.009, so SE = 0.009 / √5 ≈ 0.004, and any model scoring at least 0.781 − 0.004 = 0.777 is statistically indistinguishable from the best. Among those, the rule takes the one with the strongest penalty. It cuts the coefficients from 60 to 35.

But look at the last column. Those 35 coefficients still come from 18 of the 19 questions. LASSO drops dummy columns, not questions. It may keep region = La Araucanía and drop every other region, and the form still has to ask for the region. To remove questions you need to select whole groups of columns, which is what our forward selection did (the group LASSO does it with a penalty, but it is not in scikit-learn).

From econometrics to ML

  • OLS is unbiased; that is not the same as accurate. With many correlated regressors its variance is large. Ridge accepts a little bias to remove a lot of variance: the bias–variance trade-off from Session 3, now on coefficients.
  • scikit-learn's LogisticRegression() is already Ridge with C = 1 by default. Stata and statsmodels do not penalise. If you compare coefficients across software, this is why they differ.
  • A LASSO zero is not "not significant". It means "not needed for prediction, given the other variables". Between two correlated variables LASSO may keep one almost at random.
  • Penalised coefficients are biased by design, so the usual standard errors and p-values do not apply to them. If you need inference after selecting variables (for example, the effect of one policy variable controlling for many others), look at post-double-selection (Belloni, Chernozhukov & Hansen, 2014).

docs.title: 5. Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net, and the short form, on the test set
docs.text:
Model Questions asked CV AUC Test AUC Full form, logit (Session 5) 19 0.781 0.794 Ridge, CV-best (C = 0.32) 19 0.781 — Elastic Net (0.5), CV-best 19 0.781 — LASSO, 1-SE rule 18 0.777 0.795 Short form, forward selection 8 0.774 0.786

With 11,250 training households and 76 columns, the unpenalised logit is already stable. All three penalties tie with it on AUC. On this data shrinkage buys sparsity, not accuracy. The real choice is between the full form (0.794) and the 8-question form (0.786), which gives up 0.008 of AUC to save 11 questions per visit. That trade-off belongs to the ministry, but it can now be argued with numbers.

docs.title: 6. When does shrinkage pay off? When data is scarce
docs.text:
Imagine a pilot survey in one province: a few hundred households and the same 76 columns. We train on random subsamples of the training set (5 repetitions each) and evaluate on the full test set:

Training households No penalty Ridge (C by CV) LASSO (C by CV) 300 0.686 0.733 0.725 1,000 0.754 0.782 0.779 11,250 (all) 0.794 0.795 0.795

With 300 households the unpenalised model has 76 coefficients to estimate from about 70 poor households, and it fits the noise. The penalty cuts that variance and gains almost 0.05 of AUC. With all the data the gap disappears. The fewer observations per variable, the more the penalty is worth.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts How to avoid it Penalising unscaled variables The penalty punishes coefficients for their units, not their importance Keep StandardScaler inside the pipeline, before the model Reading C as \(\lambda\) You think you are penalising more when you are penalising less Small C = strong penalty. Plot results against C and check Selecting variables on the whole dataset, then cross-validating The selection has seen the validation folds, so the CV score is optimistic (a leak) Select inside CV on the training set; test once at the end Reading a LASSO zero as "no effect" Correlated variables share the work; LASSO keeps one Say "not needed for prediction given the others" Using l1_ratio=1 on an old scikit-learn Versions before 1.8 silently ignore it and fit a Ridge Check sklearn.__version__; count coef_ == 0 Expecting LASSO to remove questions It removes dummy columns, not whole categorical variables Select raw variables (forward selection) when the unit of cost is the question

docs.title: ✅ Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. Model A uses C = 0.01 and model B uses C = 10. Which one has more zero coefficients, and why?

Model A. \(C = 1/\lambda\), so C = 0.01 means \(\lambda = 100\), a very strong penalty, while C = 10 means \(\lambda = 0.1\). The stronger the L1 penalty, the more coefficients cannot "pay" for themselves and are set to zero. In the path widget, C = 0.01 is near the left edge, where only a handful of lines have left zero.

2. A standardised variable has \(\hat\beta = -0.35\). What are the Ridge and LASSO coefficients with \(\lambda = 0.4\)? And with \(\lambda = 0.1\)?

With \(\lambda = 0.4\): Ridge \(= -0.35 / 1.4 = -0.25\). LASSO: \(|{-0.35}| - 0.4 < 0\), so 0: the variable is dropped.

With \(\lambda = 0.1\): Ridge \(= -0.35 / 1.1 \approx -0.318\). LASSO: \(\text{sign}(-0.35) \cdot (0.35 - 0.1) = -0.25\). The sign is kept, and LASSO subtracts the same amount whatever the size of the coefficient.

3. A classmate adds income_per_capita (in pesos) and head_age (in years) to a LASSO without scaling. What goes wrong?

Two things. First, a leak: income is the variable poverty is defined from (Session 4), so it cannot be a feature at all. Second, even for legitimate variables, units: a coefficient on a variable measured in pesos is tiny (each peso matters little), so the penalty barely touches it, while a variable on a small scale needs a large coefficient and is punished hard. Selection would then depend on the units, not on how informative each variable is. Standardising puts every variable on the same footing.

4. The 1-SE LASSO has 35 non-zero coefficients but still needs 18 of the 19 questions. Explain, and suggest how to get a shorter form.

The 19 questions become 76 columns after one-hot encoding, and LASSO penalises each column separately. Keeping a single dummy of a categorical variable (one region, one household type) is enough to force the form to ask that question. To shorten the form, select whole variables: forward selection over raw variables (8 questions for CV AUC 0.774), or a group-LASSO penalty that drops all the dummies of a variable together.

5. The ministry must choose between the full form (19 questions, test AUC 0.794) and the short form (8 questions, 0.786). Give one argument for each.

For the short form: 11 fewer questions per visit means cheaper and faster targeting, so more households can be assessed with the same budget. It also leaves fewer answers an applicant can shade, and is easier to explain and audit. For the full form: the AUC gap is small on average, but at the chosen threshold it can mean a few more poor households excluded. Some dropped questions (overcrowding, dwelling type) are observable by the interviewer and hard to fake, which is valuable against manipulation even if their predictive gain is small. A good answer weighs the cost of a visit, the risk of gaming and the cost of each type of error (Session 5).

docs.text:

📓 Session 7 — Selection and Shrinkage ·

Assistant skill: debugging with the assistant instead of guessing

When something looks wrong, give the assistant the symptom, the code and your environment, and ask for a diagnosis you can check. Don't ask it to "fix it". 

I fit LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1, solver="liblinear", C=0.03) inside a Pipeline on Colab,
expecting a LASSO, but none of the 76 coefficients is exactly zero. My scikit-learn version is
(paste sklearn.__version__). Diagnose the cause. Show me the evidence: which line of the
documentation for MY version explains it, and a two-line check I can run to confirm.
Check: did it ask for (or use) your version before answering? Did it give you a check you can run (for example (model[-1].coef_ == 0).sum()), or only a confident explanation? An assistant trained on documentation of a different version will happily give you the wrong API with full confidence. That is a fabricated-API failure, and only the check catches it.

Key takeaways

  • Every variable has a cost: variance, interpretability, and in policy, collection and gaming.
  • Forward selection adds variables greedily by CV score. Select whole questions when the question is the unit of cost.
  • Ridge shrinks all coefficients, LASSO shrinks and sets some to exactly zero, and Elastic Net sits in between. Always standardise first.
  • In scikit-learn C = 1/λ: small C means a strong penalty. Choose it by CV, and when simplicity has value prefer the 1-SE model: the simplest one whose CV AUC is within one standard error (fold sd / √5) of the best.
  • Shrinkage pays off most when observations are few relative to variables. With plenty of data its gift is sparsity.
lasso = Pipeline([("pre", preprocessor(RAW)),
                  ("clf", penalised_logit(C=0.07, l1_ratio=1))])    # l1_ratio: 0 Ridge, 1 LASSO
auc = cross_val_score(lasso, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
lasso.fit(X_train, y_train)
kept = (lasso.named_steps["clf"].coef_ != 0).sum()
