docs.title: 📚 Next session
docs.text: Session 8 (Friday 20 November): so far every model has learned from a label, poor or not poor. What if we drop the label and ask the data itself: what types of households are there? Principal components and clustering, plus a project clinic.

docs.title: Session 8 · Unlabeled Data: What Types of Households Are There?
docs.text:
Friday 20 November 2026 13:00 – 16:00 Syllabus block F · Unlabeled data Checkpoint 1 feedback · project clinic Notebook Open in Colab Check your understanding

Two halves today

The first two hours cover PCA and clustering. The last 50 minutes are the project clinic: you get your Checkpoint 1 feedback and work on the final delivery with the instructor going group by group. Bring your notebook.

docs.title: ❓ Today's question
docs.text: Social programmes are designed for profiles: older people living alone, young families with children, overcrowded households. Each needs a different offer. What types of households are there, if we never tell the algorithm who is poor? And once we have them, how different is poverty from one type to another?

docs.title: 🔁 What you already know
docs.text: Everything so far was supervised: every model learned from an answer, either income (Sessions 3–4) or the label poor (Sessions 5–7). From Session 4 you know why distances need StandardScaler. From Session 2 you know groupby, which is all you need to describe a group.

docs.title: ✨ New today
docs.text: Tool What it is for Unsupervised learning Find structure in the features when there is no target PCA · explained_variance_ratio_ · components_ Summarise many correlated variables in a few new axes, and see what each axis is made of KMeans (n_clusters, n_init, random_state, inertia_) Split households into k groups of similar profiles The elbow · silhouette_score Two imperfect guides for choosing k scipy linkage · dendrogram · fcluster Hierarchical clustering, a second opinion on the same data Cluster profiling Describe each cluster in the original units, and only then look at the label

docs.title: 🗓️ Agenda (3 hours)
docs.text: Time Block 13:00 – 13:10 Recap: from supervised to unsupervised 13:10 – 14:10 PCA · k-means · choosing k 14:10 – 14:25 Break 14:25 – 15:10 Lab: profile the clusters, then look at poverty 15:10 – 16:00 Project clinic: Checkpoint 1 feedback and questions on the final delivery

docs.title: 1. No target, only features
docs.text:
In supervised learning, the error tells you whether you are right. In unsupervised learning there is no answer to check against, so the questions change:

Supervised (Sessions 3–7) Unsupervised (today) "How well do we predict poor?" "Which households resemble each other?" Test error decides No test error. Usefulness and stability decide The target guides the model The variables you choose guide the model

That last row is the key to today. We describe a household with ten variables about who lives in it and how: the head's age, schooling and weekly hours (0 if not working), female head, household size, children under 18, people over 60, rural, owns the home, overcrowded. Income and poor are never inputs. Poverty only enters at the end, to describe the groups.

One column, two meanings of missing

head_weekly_hours is missing for heads who do not work (those get 0) and for 87 working heads who did not know their hours. In the raw survey CASEN codes that "doesn't know" as −88, a trap the course file already removes. For those 87 heads, 0 would be wrong, so the notebook gives them the median hours of the people who work.

docs.title: 2. PCA: the direction of most spread
docs.text:
Picture the cloud of households on two axes, age and schooling (both standardised). Older heads had less schooling, so the cloud leans: it is long in one direction and narrow in the other. PCA rotates the axes so that the first one, PC1, runs along the long side, and PC2 is perpendicular to it. Nothing about the households changes. We only describe them in better coordinates.

Formally, PC1 is the unit vector \(w\) that maximises the variance of the projections \(z_i = w^\top x_i\). In plain words: among all ways of reducing each household to one number, PC1 keeps the most of how households differ. Each component has:

  • loadings (components_): how much each original variable contributes;
  • explained variance ratio: the share of total variance it captures;
  • scores: each household's coordinate on it.

With all ten variables, PC1 explains 31% of the variance and PC1 + PC2 together 45%:

Variable PC1 loading PC2 loading head_age 0.50 0.13 has_elderly 0.46 0.15 owns_home 0.24 0.20 household_size −0.26 0.60 has_children −0.37 0.48 overcrowded −0.16 0.36 head_schooling_years −0.34 −0.31 head_weekly_hours −0.35 −0.23

PC1 ≈ life stage: older, retired homeowners versus working heads with children. PC2 ≈ size and crowding. You need six components to pass 80%: household life does not collapse into a single index.

From econometrics to ML

  • PCA is close to factor analysis and to the indices you have seen built from survey variables. The DHS wealth index is the first principal component of household assets (Filmer & Pritchett, 2001), and PCA-based welfare indices are themselves used for targeting.
  • PCs are uncorrelated by construction. Using the first few as regressors is principal components regression (ISLR §6.3), a remedy for multicollinearity.
  • A component has no causal meaning. "Life stage" is a name we give to a direction.
  • Clustering has no ground truth: unlike a regression, there is no residual or test error that says you got it right. You judge clusters by stability and by usefulness.

docs.title: 3. k-means: assign, update, repeat
docs.text:
k-means looks for k groups whose members are close to their group's centre, the centroid. It alternates two steps until nobody switches:

  1. Assign each household to its nearest centroid.
  2. Update each centroid to the mean of its households.

Each step can only lower the inertia, the total squared distance from households to their centroids: \(\sum_i \lVert x_i - \mu_{c(i)} \rVert^2\). Press Step and watch both moves on real households, drawn on the first two principal components:

Worked example by hand

Six households, two standardised variables: age of head (\(z_\text{age}\), positive = older) and household size (\(z_\text{size}\), positive = larger). k = 2, starting centroids at households A and D.

A B C D E F \(z_\text{age}\) 1.0 1.2 0.8 −1.0 −0.6 0.2 \(z_\text{size}\) −0.5 −1.0 0.0 1.0 0.4 0.6

Assign. Squared distance to \(c_1 = (1.0, -0.5)\) and to \(c_2 = (-1.0, 1.0)\):

  • B: \((0.2^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.29\) vs \((2.2^2 + 2.0^2) = 8.84\) → cluster 1
  • C: \((0.2^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.29\) vs \((1.8^2 + 1.0^2) = 4.24\) → cluster 1
  • E: \((1.6^2 + 0.9^2) = 3.37\) vs \((0.4^2 + 0.6^2) = 0.52\) → cluster 2
  • F: \((0.8^2 + 1.1^2) = 1.85\) vs \((1.2^2 + 0.4^2) = 1.60\) → cluster 2 (a close call)

Update. Cluster 1 = {A, B, C}: \(c_1 = \big(\tfrac{1.0+1.2+0.8}{3}, \tfrac{-0.5-1.0+0.0}{3}\big) = (1.0, -0.5)\). Cluster 2 = {D, E, F}: \(c_2 = \big(\tfrac{-1.0-0.6+0.2}{3}, \tfrac{1.0+0.4+0.6}{3}\big) = (-0.47, 0.67)\).

Assign again. F is now at \(0.45\) from \(c_2\) and \(1.85\) from \(c_1\), so it stays. Nobody switches: converged. Inertia \(= 0.58 + 0.93 = 1.51\).

Reading: cluster 1 is older, smaller households; cluster 2 is younger, larger households.

docs.title: 4. Local minima: why n_init matters
docs.text: k-means only ever moves "downhill" from where it starts, so a bad start can leave it stuck. With k = 4 and one run per seed, five seeds give inertias from 87,198 to 95,803 and visibly different clusters. n_init=50 runs the algorithm 50 times and keeps the run with the lowest inertia. On this data, n_init=10 with random_state=42 still ends in a worse solution (90,043), so we use 50. Report n_init and random_state with every clustering result.

docs.title: 5. Choosing k
docs.text:
Inertia always falls as k grows: with k = 15,000, every household is its own cluster. So we look for an elbow, where extra clusters stop paying off. The silhouette compares, for each household, the mean distance to its own cluster (\(a\)) with the mean distance to the nearest other cluster (\(b\)): \(s = (b - a) / \max(a, b)\). It runs from −1 to 1, and higher means better separated.

k Inertia Silhouette 2 114,527 0.228 3 99,309 0.251 4 87,197 0.219 5 78,908 0.218 6 73,732 0.217

An honest reading: there is no sharp elbow, and every silhouette is low. Households form a continuum, not islands. That is normal with social data, and you should say so. The silhouette prefers k = 3, but k = 3 puts families with and without children in one group (57% with children), which is exactly the distinction a family programme cares about. Going from 3 to 4 clusters still cuts inertia by 12,100, while from 4 to 5 the gain drops to 8,300. We take k = 4, and we say why.

docs.title: 6. Profile first, then look at poverty
docs.text:
A cluster is a number until you describe it in the original units:

Older households Families with children Working adults, no children Overcrowded families Households 5,888 4,599 3,934 579 Age of head 70 43 46 42 Weekly hours worked 9 33 37 31 With children 8% 100% 0% 89% With someone 60+ 97% 13% 13% 20% Owns the home 80% 52% 45% 32% Overcrowded 0% 0% 0% 100% Poverty rate (revealed last) 23.7% 26.4% 15.8% 40.2%

The algorithm never saw who is poor, yet poverty ranges from 16% to 40% across the clusters (23.1% overall). Two cautions:

  • This is description, not explanation. Clusters do not say why a household is poor.
  • The overcrowded cluster has the highest rate but holds only 233 of 3,464 poor households (7%). A subsidy aimed at that cluster alone would miss 93% of the poor. Targeting is the job of the supervised models from Sessions 5–7. Clusters help design what to offer each group.

docs.title: 7. Hierarchical clustering: a second opinion
docs.text: Agglomerative clustering starts with every household on its own and repeatedly merges the two closest groups. With Ward linkage, "closest" means the merge that increases within-cluster variance the least, the same objective as k-means. The dendrogram shows the whole merge history, and cutting it at a height gives clusters. It needs every pairwise distance, so the notebook uses 500 households. Cut into four groups, 437 of 500 (87%) fall into clusters that match the k-means ones: two algorithms, same four profiles. The disagreements are households that sit between profiles.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it hurts How to avoid Clustering unscaled variables Age (sd 16.5) and hours (sd 22.7) decide everything; unscaled k = 4 just splits by age and hours worked StandardScaler before PCA and k-means Putting income or poor in the inputs You "discover" poverty segments you built in Keep the label out; attach it only after clustering One run, default seed Local minima: different clusters every time n_init=50, fixed random_state, report both Treating a silhouette of 0.2 as "clear types" It signals a continuum, not separate groups Say how weak the structure is; check stability Ignoring rare 0/1 variables After scaling, a 1 in overcrowded (4% of households) becomes z ≈ 5 and grabs a cluster Decide deliberately whether that segment is what you want Naming clusters as natural or causal types "Life stage causes poverty" is not in the data Names are labels for discussion, not findings

docs.title: ✅ Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. Why must you standardise before PCA? What would PC1 be on the raw variables?

PCA looks for the direction of largest variance. On raw data, variance depends on units: head_weekly_hours has a standard deviation of about 23 and head_age about 16.5, while the 0/1 variables are below 0.5. PC1 would essentially be "hours and age" because those numbers are bigger, not because they matter more. Standardising gives every variable variance 1, so PCA finds shared patterns rather than large units.

2. Two standardised variables have correlation r = −0.6. What share of the variance does PC1 keep?

With two standardised variables, PC1 keeps \((1 + |r|)/2 = (1 + 0.6)/2 = 0.80\), or 80%. The sign does not matter, only the strength. With r = 0 it would keep 50%: no direction is better than another. In our data r = −0.498, so PC1 keeps 74.9%.

3. Redo the worked example starting from centroids B and F. Where does it end?

First assignment: A goes to B (0.29 vs 1.85), C goes to F (1.16 vs 0.72), D and E go to F. So cluster 1 = {A, B}, cluster 2 = {C, D, E, F}. Update: \(c_1 = (1.1, -0.75)\), \(c_2 = (-0.15, 0.5)\). Assign again: C is now at 0.65 from \(c_1\) and 1.15 from \(c_2\), so it switches. One more update gives exactly the first solution, {A, B, C} and {D, E, F}, with inertia 1.51. Different starts can take different paths. On real data they can also end in different places, which is why we use n_init.

4. The silhouette is highest at k = 3. Isn't choosing k = 4 cheating?

No, as long as you say so. Neither criterion is a test: all silhouettes are low (0.21–0.25), and the elbow is soft. k = 4 separates families with and without children, a distinction with direct policy use, and the inertia gain from 3 to 4 (12,100) is still clearly larger than from 4 to 5 (8,300). Cheating would be reporting k = 4 as "what the data says" and hiding the silhouette.

5. A minister proposes paying the subsidy only to the 'overcrowded families' cluster, since 40% of them are poor. What do you answer?

That cluster contains 233 of the 3,464 poor households in the sample: about 7%. Used as a targeting rule, it would have a recall of 0.07, far below the Session 5 logit at any sensible threshold, and it would still pay 346 non-poor households. The clusters are useful to design the offer (overcrowded families may need housing support more than cash). Deciding who gets the subsidy is a prediction problem, and Sessions 5–7 handle it with the right metrics.

docs.title: 🧪 Lab
docs.text:
The notebook rebuilds every number on this page: the -88 fix, PCA, the local-minimum demo, the choice of k, the profiles, poverty by cluster, the unscaled comparison and the dendrogram.

📓 Session 8 — Unlabeled Data ·

Assistant skill: review the plot, not just the code

I clustered 15,000 Chilean households into 4 groups with k-means on 10 standardised variables
(paste the list). Write code for (1) a scatter of the first two PCA scores coloured by cluster,
with the explained variance in each axis label, and (2) a bar chart of the cluster profiles in
the original units. Then describe each cluster in one sentence.
Then check, line by line:

  • Do the axis labels show the real explained variance (31% and 15%)?
  • Is the profile chart in original units or z-scores, and does it say which?
  • Is every claim in its descriptions backed by a number in your profile table?
  • Did it call the clusters "natural types", or suggest they cause poverty?

Every correction goes into your assistant log.

Key takeaways

  • Unsupervised learning has no target and no test error. The variables you choose define the answer, so choose them deliberately and keep the label out.
  • PCA rotates standardised data onto directions of maximum variance. Read the loadings to name a component, and the explained variance to know how much it keeps.
  • k-means alternates assign and update. It finds a local minimum, so run it many times (n_init) with a fixed random_state.
  • Choose k with the elbow, the silhouette and the use you will give the segments, and report all three.
  • Profile clusters in the original units first, and attach the label only afterwards. Clusters describe; they do not target and do not explain.
Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(F)                       # F: features, never the label
pca = PCA().fit(Z); pca.explained_variance_ratio_
km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=50, random_state=42).fit(Z)
silhouette_score(Z[sample], km.labels_[sample])
F.assign(cluster=km.labels_).groupby("cluster").mean()      # profile, then add df["poor"]

docs.title: ❓ Today's question
docs.text: You have built a model on a real problem. Can you convince a decision-maker to use it, and defend every choice behind it?

docs.title: 🗓️ Agenda (3 hours)
docs.text: Time Block 13:00 – 13:10 Order of presentations (drawn at random) 13:10 – 15:40 Presentations: 12 minutes + 5 minutes of questions per group, with a break halfway 15:40 – 16:00 Course closing

docs.title: How to structure 12 minutes
docs.text:
A decision-maker remembers three things: the problem, what your model changes, and whether they can trust it. A structure that works:

Minutes Slide(s) What it must answer 1.5 The decision Who decides what with your prediction? What does each kind of error cost? 1.5 The data Unit of analysis, rows, target, and what you would not have at prediction time 3 The honest comparison Baseline vs. your models, same CV folds, mean ± spread. One table or one chart, not five 2 The choice Which model you would deploy, and why: not only the highest score 2.5 The recommendation What changes because of the model, quantified, with explicit assumptions 1.5 Limits What would break in production, and what data you would need next

One number per slide

If a slide needs a pointer to explain, it has too much on it. The chart that compares your models is the most important one in the talk; give it the most time.

docs.title: The questions you will be asked
docs.text:
Questions are about your code and your choices. Every member of the group must be able to answer them. Expect questions like these:

  • Show me where you split the data. What happens to the test set after that line?
  • Which steps are inside your pipeline? What would change if this one were outside?
  • Why this metric, and why this threshold? What would a 1:1 cost ratio change?
  • Pick one feature: would you really know its value when the decision is made?
  • Your best model beats the baseline by X. Is that more than the spread across folds?
  • What did the assistant get wrong, and how did you notice? (from your assistant log)

Code you cannot explain is code you did not write

This is the core of the assessment. If a group member cannot explain a part of the notebook, that part counts as not done, whoever (or whatever) wrote it.

docs.title: ✅ Final checklist
docs.text:
• The notebook runs from top to bottom after Restart & Run all.
  • The baseline appears next to every model score.
  • Every model was compared on the same cross-validation folds; the test set was used once.
  • The threshold (if classification) is justified with the costs of each error.
  • The report states assumptions and limitations explicitly.
  • The assistant log has real entries, including what you rejected or corrected.
  • You responded to the Checkpoint 1 feedback, and the report says how.

docs.title: Course closing: what you can now do
docs.text:
Look back at the case. Starting from a survey file, you have:

Session You learned to… 1–2 Read a dataset by its types and turn it into one clean row per household 3 Fit a model, and see why fitting the training data says nothing 4 Report an error you can defend: pipelines, cross-validation, no leakage 5 Turn probabilities into decisions, and price each kind of mistake 6 Use flexible models (trees and ensembles), and weigh accuracy against explainability 7 Ask which variables are worth collecting, and shrink the rest 8 Find structure without labels, and use it to design policy

Throughout, you wrote less code by hand than any cohort before you, and you had to review more of it. That habit of verifying is the part that will not go out of date.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Text and naïve Bayes, and neural networks: ISLR chapters 4.4 and 10, at the same level as this course.
  • Causal machine learning: when the question is "what is the effect of the programme?" rather than "who is poor?". Look for double/debiased machine learning (Chernozhukov et al., 2018).
  • Targeting in practice: compare your proxy means test with the community-based and self-targeting approaches discussed in the development literature.

Thank you for a great term. 🎓

docs.title: Grading Rubric¶
docs.text:
The 100 points for this project will be divided as follows, with each category evaluated at three levels: Achieved, Partially Achieved, and Not Achieved.

  1. Data Selection and Cleaning (20 points)

    • Achieved (20 points): Relevant dataset with appropriate cleaning and preprocessing.
    • Partially Achieved (10-15 points): Dataset is relevant but requires more thorough cleaning or preprocessing.
    • Not Achieved (0-9 points): Dataset is not relevant or poorly cleaned/preprocessed.

  2. Data Analysis and Variable Selection (20 points)

    • Achieved (20 points): Comprehensive analysis and appropriate variable selection for the model.
    • Partially Achieved (10-15 points): Basic analysis conducted; variable selection could be improved.
    • Not Achieved (0-9 points): Inadequate analysis and poor variable selection.

  3. Model Implementation and Testing (30 points)

    • Achieved (30 points): Accurate implementation and testing of all required models with a well-constructed comparative table.
    • Partially Achieved (15-25 points): Implementation and testing of most models; comparative table lacks detail.
    • Not Achieved (0-14 points): Incomplete model implementation or testing; no comparative table.

  4. K-means Clustering Analysis (20 points)

    • Achieved (20 points): Effective use of K-means clustering with clear explanations of each cluster.
    • Partially Achieved (10-15 points): Basic use of K-means clustering; explanations of clusters are vague.
    • Not Achieved (0-9 points): Poor or no use of K-means clustering; no explanations of clusters.

  5. Oral Presentation (10 points)

    • Achieved (10 points): Clear, concise, and well-organized presentation within the time limit.
    • Partially Achieved (5-9 points): Presentation is understandable but could be more organized or better timed.
    • Not Achieved (0-4 points): Unclear or disorganized presentation; significantly exceeds or falls short of the time limit.

docs.title: Dealing with Missing Data in a Dataset¶
Identifying Missing Data¶
docs.text:
The first step in dealing with missing data is to identify its presence and location within your dataset. This can be done using various methods, depending on the tools and programming language you are using. In Python, for instance, you can use libraries like Pandas to easily find missing values.

import pandas as pd


# Assuming 'df' is your DataFrame

missing_values = df.isnull()

print(missing_values.sum())

This code will give you a count of missing values in each column of your DataFrame.

docs.title: Handling Missing Data¶
docs.text: Once you've identified the missing data, the next step is to decide how to handle it. The approach depends on the nature of your data and the amount of missing information. Here are some common strategies:

docs.title: 1. Removing Data¶
docs.text:
• Drop rows with missing values: If the dataset is large and the number of rows with missing data is small, you might consider removing these rows.
df.dropna(inplace=True)
  • Drop columns with missing values: If a specific column has a significant number of missing values, it might be better to remove the entire column.
df.dropna(axis=1, inplace=True)

docs.title: 2. Imputing Data¶
docs.text:
• Mean/Median/Mode Imputation: Replace missing values with the mean, median, or mode of the column. This is useful for numerical data.
# For mean imputation

df.fillna(df.mean(), inplace=True)


# For median imputation

df.fillna(df.median(), inplace=True)


# For mode imputation (for categorical data)

df.fillna(df.mode().iloc[0], inplace=True)
  • Custom Imputation: Use domain knowledge or other algorithms to impute missing values.

docs.title: 3. Using Algorithms that Support Missing Values¶
docs.text: • Some machine learning algorithms can handle missing values inherently. For example, decision trees and random forests can handle missing data without imputation.

docs.title: Dealing with Outliers in a Dataset¶
Understanding and Handling Outliers¶
docs.text: Outliers are data points that differ significantly from other observations. They can occur due to variability in the measurement or may indicate experimental errors. Handling outliers is crucial as they can lead to misleading representations and affect the results of data analysis.

docs.title: Steps to Handle Outliers:¶
docs.text:
1. Visualizing Data: Using plots like boxplots to identify outliers.

  2. Identifying Outliers: Determining which data points are considered outliers.

  3. Removing Outliers: Deciding on a strategy to handle outliers, often by removing them.

We will demonstrate these steps using a dataset with more than 50 rows, analyze it with a boxplot, identify outliers, and then remove them.

docs.title: Selecting Variables for a Classification Model¶
Selecting Variables for Classification Using the Iris Dataset¶
docs.text: In this section, we will demonstrate how to select variables for a classification model using the Iris dataset. This dataset is a classic in machine learning, featuring measurements of iris flowers and their species. We will explore different techniques to determine which features are most important for classification.

docs.title: Feature Selection Using Random Forest on the Wine Dataset¶
docs.text: Another popular technique for feature selection is using a Random Forest classifier. This method is particularly useful for understanding feature importance in classification tasks. We will use the Wine dataset, another classic dataset in machine learning, to demonstrate this technique.

docs.title: Conclusion on Feature Selection for the Wine Dataset¶
docs.text: Based on the feature importance rankings and the visual representation, we can conclude which features are most significant for the classification model. Generally, features with higher importance scores are more influential in predicting the target variable. In this case, we would select the top-ranking features as they have the highest impact on the model's performance.

docs.title: Feature Selection Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the Breast Cancer Dataset¶
docs.text: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a technique used for dimensionality reduction, which can also be helpful in feature selection. It transforms the data into a new set of variables, the principal components, which are orthogonal and uncorrelated. We will use the Breast Cancer dataset to demonstrate this technique.

docs.title: Conclusion on Feature Selection with PCA¶
docs.text: After applying PCA to the Breast Cancer dataset, we can observe how the data is distributed across the principal components. PCA helps in reducing the dimensionality of the dataset while retaining the most significant features. In this case, we transformed the data into two principal components. These components can be used for further analysis or in building classification models, as they encapsulate the most variance of the dataset.

docs.title: Self-Learning Lab: Python Dataframes with Examples
Self-Learning Lab: Python Dataframes with Examples¶
docs.text: Welcome to this self-learning lab on Python Dataframes! In this lab, you will explore and practice key concepts related to dataframes using the pandas library. The lab is designed to be completed in approximately two hours. For each topic, we will provide a brief overview, an example, and then an exercise for you to complete. The exercises are designed with a business context in mind, so you'll be able to apply these concepts in real-world scenarios.

docs.title: Contents:¶
docs.text:
1. Introduction to Dataframes in Pandas
  2. Data Transformation: Creating New Columns
  3. Filtering and Indexing in Dataframes
  4. The apply Function and Lambda Expressions
  5. One Hot Encoding Let's dive in!

docs.title: 1. Introduction to Dataframes in Pandas¶
docs.text: A DataFrame is a 2-dimensional labeled data structure with columns that can be of different types. It is similar to a spreadsheet, a SQL table, or the data.frame in R. The DataFrame is one of the most commonly used pandas objects and is designed to handle a mix of numeric and non-numeric data.

docs.title: Example:¶
docs.text:
Let's create a simple dataframe with product sales data.

import pandas as pd
data = {
    'Product Name': ['Laptop', 'Mouse', 'Keyboard'],
    'Units Sold': [50, 150, 80],
    'Price per Unit': [800, 20, 30]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

docs.title: Exercise 1.1:¶
docs.text:
Imagine you are a data analyst at a retail company. You have been given sales data for the past month. The data includes the product name, the number of units sold, and the price per unit. Using the pandas library, create a dataframe with the following data:

Product Name Units Sold Price per Unit Laptop 50 800 Mouse 150 20 Keyboard 80 30

Calculate the total sales for each product and add it as a new column to the dataframe.

docs.title: 2. Data Transformation: Creating New Columns¶
docs.text: Often, while working with data, you might want to create new columns based on the existing columns in the dataframe. This can be done using various operations and functions.

docs.title: Example:¶
docs.text:
Given the sales data, let's calculate the total sales for each product.

df['Total Sales'] = df['Units Sold'] * df['Price per Unit']
print(df)

docs.title: Exercise 2.1:¶
docs.text:
Continuing with the retail company scenario, let's say you have been given additional data regarding the cost of each product. You are required to calculate the profit for each product. Add the following data to your dataframe:

Product Name Cost per Unit Laptop 600 Mouse 10 Keyboard 20

Create a new column in the dataframe to calculate the profit for each product. Profit is calculated as (Price per Unit - Cost per Unit) * Units Sold.

docs.title: 3. Filtering and Indexing in Dataframes¶
docs.text: Filtering allows you to select specific rows based on a condition. Indexing, on the other hand, helps in selecting specific rows and columns from the dataframe.

docs.title: Example:¶
docs.text:
From the sales data, let's extract the details of products that have sold more than 100 units.

high_selling_products = df[df['Units Sold'] > 100]
print(high_selling_products[['Product Name', 'Units Sold']])

docs.title: Exercise 3.1:¶
docs.text: From the sales data, extract the details of products that have sold more than 100 units. Display only the 'Product Name' and 'Units Sold' columns.

docs.title: Exercise 3.2:¶
docs.text: From the sales data, extract the details of the product that has the highest profit. Display the 'Product Name' and 'Profit' columns.

docs.title: 4. The apply Function and Lambda Expressions¶
docs.text: The apply function is used to apply a function along the axis of the dataframe. Lambda expressions are small anonymous functions that can be used with functions like apply.

docs.title: Example:¶
docs.text:
Using the sales data, let's create a new column 'Category' that categorizes products as 'High Selling' if units sold are greater than 100, and 'Low Selling' otherwise.

df['Category'] = df['Units Sold'].apply(lambda x: 'High Selling' if x > 100 else 'Low Selling')
print(df[['Product Name', 'Category']])

docs.title: 5. One Hot Encoding¶
docs.text: One hot encoding is a process of converting categorical data variables so they can be provided to machine learning algorithms to improve predictions. It involves converting each value in a column to a new column and assigning a 1 or 0 (True/False) value to the column.

docs.title: Example:¶
docs.text:
Using the sales data, let's one-hot encode the 'Category' column.

encoded_df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['Category'])
print(encoded_df)

docs.title: S01 types of data
docs.text:
In the field of data science, we often talk about different types of data. Understanding these types is crucial for proper data analysis and interpretation. Here are some of the most common types of data:

  1. Numerical Data: This type of data is quantitative and can be divided into two types: discrete and continuous. Discrete numerical data is countable (e.g., the number of employees in a company), while continuous numerical data can take any value within a range (e.g., the weight of a person).

  2. Categorical Data: This type of data is qualitative and describes categories or groups (e.g., the color of a car). It can be further divided into nominal data (no order implied) and ordinal data (order is significant).

  3. Binary Data: A special case of categorical data where the variable has only two categories or groups (e.g., yes/no, true/false).

  4. Time-series Data: This type of data is collected over time and the order of the data points is important (e.g., stock prices over time).

  5. Text Data: This type of data is unstructured and is typically in the form of sentences or paragraphs (e.g., customer reviews).

In Python, we have several data types that are commonly used. Here are some of them with examples:

  1. Integers: These are whole numbers. For example, 5, 10, -1.

  2. Floats: These are real numbers (i.e., numbers that can have a decimal point). For example, 5.0, 1.23, -0.5.

  3. Strings: These are sequences of characters. For example, 'Hello, World!', 'Python'.

  4. Booleans: These represent truth values True and False.

  5. Lists: These are ordered collections of items (which can be of different types). For example, [1, 2, 3], ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'].

  6. Tuples: These are like lists, but they are immutable (i.e., they can't be modified after they are created). For example, (1, 2, 3), ('apple', 'banana', 'cherry').

  7. Dictionaries: These are collections of key-value pairs. For example, {'name': 'John', 'age': 30}.

Python has a variety of operators that can be used with different data types. Here are some examples:

  1. Arithmetic Operators: These are used with numeric values to perform common mathematical operations.

    • Addition: 5 + 3 returns 8
    • Subtraction: 5 - 3 returns 2
    • Multiplication: 5 * 3 returns 15
    • Division: 5 / 3 returns 1.6666666666666667
    • Modulus: 5 % 3 returns 2
    • Exponentiation: 5 ** 3 returns 125
    • Floor division: 5 // 3 returns 1

  2. Comparison Operators: These are used to compare two values.

    • Equal: 5 == 3 returns False
    • Not equal: 5 != 3 returns True
    • Greater than: 5 > 3 returns True
    • Less than: 5 < 3 returns False
    • Greater than or equal to: 5 >= 3 returns True
    • Less than or equal to: 5 <= 3 returns False

  3. Logical Operators: These are used to combine conditional statements.

    • and: Returns True if both statements are true
    • or: Returns True if one of the statements is true
    • not: Reverse the result, returns False if the result is true

  4. Membership Operators: These are used to test if a sequence is presented in an object.

    • in: Returns True if a sequence with the specified value is present in the object
    • not in: Returns True if a sequence with the specified value is not present in the object

  5. String Operators: Python also has a set of operators that are specifically designed to work with strings. These include the + operator for concatenation and the * operator for repetition.

In Python, a function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task. Functions help break our program into smaller and modular chunks, making it organized and manageable. They also prevent repetition and make the code reusable.

Here's the basic syntax of a Python function:

def function_name(parameters):
    """docstring"""
    statement(s)
  1. The def keyword is a statement for defining a function in Python.
  2. function_name is a unique identifier for the function.
  3. parameters (arguments) through which we pass values to a function. These are optional.
  4. A colon (:) to mark the end of the function header.
  5. Optional documentation string (docstring) to describe what the function does.
  6. One or more valid python statements that make up the function body. Statements must have the same indentation level (usually 4 spaces).
  7. An optional return statement to return a value from the function.
In [ ]: Copied! 
# Example of a Python function

def greet(name):
    """
    This function greets the person passed in as a parameter
    """
    print(f'Hello, {name}. Good morning!')

# Calling the function
greet('John')
# Example of a Python function def greet(name): """ This function greets the person passed in as a parameter """ print(f'Hello, {name}. Good morning!') # Calling the function greet('John') 
Hello, John. Good morning!
In [ ]: Copied! 
# Example of a Python function with a return statement

def add_numbers(num1, num2):
    """
    This function adds the two numbers passed in as parameters
    """
    return num1 + num2

# Calling the function and printing the result
result = add_numbers(5, 3)
print(f'The sum is {result}')
# Example of a Python function with a return statement def add_numbers(num1, num2): """ This function adds the two numbers passed in as parameters """ return num1 + num2 # Calling the function and printing the result result = add_numbers(5, 3) print(f'The sum is {result}') 
The sum is 8

docs.title: S02 data manipulation
docs.text:
A DataFrame is a two-dimensional, size-mutable, and heterogeneous tabular data structure with labeled axes (rows and columns). It is one of the most commonly used data structures in data analysis and machine learning, especially when dealing with structured data.

In [ ]: Copied! 
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Creating a fictitious sales data
np.random.seed(42)
data = {
    'Product ID': np.arange(1, 101),
    'Product Name': ['Product_' + str(i) for i in range(1, 101)],
    'Category': np.random.choice(['Electronics', 'Clothing', 'Groceries', 'Household'], 100),
    'Price': np.random.uniform(10, 500, 100).round(2),
    'Units Sold': np.random.randint(1, 100, 100),
    'Date of Sale': pd.date_range(start='2022-01-01', periods=100, freq='D')
}

# Introducing some missing values
for _ in range(10):
    data['Price'][np.random.randint(0, 100)] = np.nan
    data['Units Sold'][np.random.randint(0, 100)] = np.nan

sales_df = pd.DataFrame(data)
sales_df.head()

  • Revenue: The average revenue of the companies listed is approximately 8,488.47 million. The minimum revenue is 0 million (which might indicate missing or unreported data for some companies), and the maximum revenue is a staggering 559,151 million. # Calculating the correlation matrix correlation_matrix = fortune_df.corr() # Plotting the correlation heatmap plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) sns.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm', linewidths=0.5, vmin=-1, vmax=1) plt.title('Correlation Heatmap') plt.tight_layout() plt.show()

From the correlation heatmap, we can observe the following:

  • Year and Rank: There's a negative correlation between the year and the rank. This might indicate that over the years, the ranking criteria or the companies in the list have changed.
  • Revenue and Rank: There's also a negative correlation between revenue and rank. This is expected since a higher revenue would generally mean a higher rank (or a lower rank number) on the Fortune 500 list.

It's important to note that correlation does not imply causation. While these variables might be correlated, it doesn't mean that one causes the other. The heatmap provides a quick overview of potential relationships that might be worth exploring further.

docs.title: Why are DataFrames important?¶
docs.text:
• Structured Representation: DataFrames provide a structured representation of data, making it easier to observe and analyze.
  • Flexibility: They can hold different types of data (e.g., integer, string, float) in different columns.
  • Functionality: Libraries like pandas in Python offer a wide range of functions to manipulate, filter, group, and transform data in DataFrames.
  • Integration with Machine Learning: DataFrames are often used as input data structures for machine learning models. They can be easily split into training and testing sets, and their columns can be used as features for models.

docs.title: Applications in Data Analysis and Machine Learning¶
docs.text:
1. Data Cleaning: Handling missing values, filtering rows or columns, and transforming data.
  2. Data Exploration: Calculating statistics, visualizing data, and identifying patterns.
  3. Feature Engineering: Creating new features from existing ones to improve model performance.
  4. Model Training: Using DataFrames to train machine learning models.

docs.title: Business Example¶
docs.text:
Imagine a retail company that wants to analyze its sales data. The data might include columns like 'Product ID', 'Product Name', 'Category', 'Price', 'Units Sold', and 'Date of Sale'. With a DataFrame, the company can easily:

  • Analyze sales trends over time.
  • Identify the best-selling products.
  • Calculate the total revenue for a specific time period.
  • Group sales data by category or product.
  • Predict future sales using machine learning models.

docs.title: Descripción de las Columnas¶
docs.text:
• Year: Esta columna representa el año en el que se registraron los datos de la empresa. Es de tipo int64, lo que significa que contiene valores enteros.

  • Name: Esta columna contiene el nombre de la empresa. Es de tipo object, lo que generalmente indica que contiene cadenas de texto.

  • Revenue: Esta columna representa los ingresos de la empresa en millones. Es de tipo float64, lo que indica que contiene valores decimales.

Cada columna tiene un significado específico y es esencial para el análisis de las empresas Fortune 500 y su rendimiento a lo largo de los años.

import numpy as np

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

    plt.xlabel("x")
    plt.ylabel("y")
    plt.xlim((0, 5))
    plt.ylim((-2, 2))
    plt.legend(loc="best")

docs.title: Machine Learning Models¶
docs.text: In the realm of data science and artificial intelligence, machine learning models play a pivotal role. They are algorithms that learn patterns from data and then make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed to do so. In the business context, machine learning models can be used for a variety of tasks such as customer segmentation, sales forecasting, and even fraud detection.

docs.title: What is a ML Model?¶
docs.text: A machine learning model is a mathematical representation of a real-world process. Think of it as a mathematical equation that has been trained on historical data to make predictions about future data. For businesses, these models can be used to gain insights, make informed decisions, and automate tasks.

docs.title: Fitting a Model¶
docs.text:
Fitting a model, also known as training a model, involves providing a machine learning algorithm with data and allowing it to learn the patterns. This is done by feeding the model input data and the corresponding output. The model then adjusts its weights based on the error of its predictions. In a business scenario, this could mean using past sales data to predict future sales.

In the following sections, we will delve deeper into specific machine learning models and their applications in the business world.

docs.title: KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors)¶
docs.text: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is a simple, yet powerful supervised machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression. It works by finding the 'k' training examples that are closest to a given input example and returning the most common output value among them.

docs.title: Business Application of KNN¶
docs.text:
Imagine a retail business that wants to segment its customers based on their purchase behavior. Using KNN, the business can classify a new customer into a particular segment by looking at the purchase behaviors of the 'k' most similar existing customers. This can help the business tailor its marketing strategies for different customer segments.

Let's see a simple example in Python where we use KNN to classify customers into two segments: 'High Value' and 'Low Value' based on their annual spending and frequency of purchase.

docs.title: Polynomial Regression¶
docs.text: Polynomial Regression is a type of regression analysis used to model the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables by fitting a polynomial equation to the observed data. Unlike linear regression which models the relationship using a straight line, polynomial regression models it using a curve.

docs.title: Business Application of Polynomial Regression¶
docs.text:
Consider a business that wants to understand the relationship between advertising spend and sales. While initially, an increase in advertising might lead to a significant increase in sales, after a certain point, the effect of additional advertising might diminish. In such cases, a polynomial regression can capture the non-linear relationship between advertising spend and sales more effectively than a linear model.

Let's see a Python example where we use Polynomial Regression to model the relationship between advertising spend and sales.

docs.title: Advanced KNN Example: Loan Default Prediction¶
docs.text:
In this scenario, a bank wants to predict the risk associated with a loan based on a customer's credit score and annual income. The bank classifies the risk into three categories: 'Low Risk', 'Medium Risk', and 'High Risk'.

Let's use KNN to classify customers into these risk categories.

docs.title: Advanced Polynomial Regression Example: Salary Prediction¶
docs.text:
In this scenario, a company wants to understand the relationship between the years of experience and the salary of its employees. As employees gain more experience, the growth in their salary might not be linear, especially at higher experience levels where salary increments might start to plateau.

Let's use Polynomial Regression to model this non-linear relationship between years of experience and salary.

docs.title: KNN Exercise: Customer Churn Prediction¶
docs.text: In this exercise, you'll be working with a fictional dataset representing a company's customer data. Your task is to predict customer churn, i.e., the likelihood of a customer leaving the company's services, based on their usage metrics and demographic information.

docs.title: Dataset Description¶
docs.text:
• Age: Age of the customer (numeric)
  • MonthlyCharge: Monthly charge for the services (numeric, in $)
  • CustomerServiceCalls: Number of calls made to customer service (numeric)
  • Churn: Whether the customer left the company within the last month (0 for No, 1 for Yes)

docs.title: Objective¶
docs.text:
Using the KNN algorithm, classify customers into 'Churn' or 'No Churn' based on the given features.

Let's get started!

docs.title: Data Preparation¶
docs.text:
Before applying the KNN algorithm, we need to prepare our data. This involves:

  1. Splitting the data into features (X) and target label (y). In our case, 'Age', 'MonthlyCharge', and 'CustomerServiceCalls' are our features, and 'Churn' is our target label.
  2. Splitting the dataset into training and testing sets. This allows us to train our model on one subset and test its performance on another unseen subset.

Let's perform these steps.

docs.title: Applying the KNN Algorithm¶
docs.text:
Now that our data is prepared, we can apply the KNN algorithm. Here are the steps we'll follow:

  1. Initialize the KNN Classifier: We'll use the KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn to create our KNN model. The key parameter here is n_neighbors, which represents the number of neighbors to consider when making a prediction.
  2. Train the Classifier: We'll use the fit method to train our KNN classifier on the training data.
  3. Make Predictions: Once trained, we can use the predict method to make predictions on new, unseen data.

Let's go through each step with code and explanations.

docs.title: Making Predictions with the KNN Classifier¶
docs.text:
Now that our KNN classifier is trained, we can use it to make predictions on new data. For this exercise, we'll predict the churn for the test data and then compare these predictions to the actual churn values to evaluate the performance of our model.

To make predictions, we'll use the predict method of our trained KNN classifier. This method takes in the features of the data we want to predict and returns the predicted labels.

Let's make predictions on our test data and display the results.

docs.title: Overfitting and Underfitting: Bias versus Variance¶
docs.text:
In machine learning, achieving the right balance between bias and variance is crucial for creating models that generalize well to new, unseen data. Let's delve into these concepts:

  • Bias: Refers to the error introduced by approximating a real-world problem (which may be complex) by a too-simple model. High bias can cause the model to miss relevant relations between features and target outputs, leading to underfitting.

  • Variance: Refers to the error introduced by using a model that's too complex. High variance can cause the model to model the random noise in the training data, leading to overfitting.

docs.title: Underfitting:¶
docs.text: Occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying structure of the data. Such a model has high bias and low variance.

docs.title: Overfitting:¶
docs.text:
Occurs when a model is too complex and fits the training data too closely, including its noise and outliers. Such a model has low bias and high variance.

The goal in machine learning is to achieve a balance between bias and variance, ensuring that the model is flexible enough to model the data's structure but not so flexible that it fits the noise in the data.

Let's visualize the concepts of overfitting and underfitting.

docs.title: The Cost Function¶
docs.text:
In machine learning, the cost function (or loss function) quantifies how well the model's predictions match the actual values. In other words, it measures the error of the model. The goal during training is to minimize this error.

For linear regression, a common cost function is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), which calculates the average of the squared differences between the predicted and actual values.

The formula for MSE is:

$$ MSE = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 $$

Where:

  • $y_i$ is the actual value.
  • $\hat{y}_i$ is the predicted value.
  • $ n $ is the number of observations.

Let's implement the MSE in Python and calculate it for a sample set of actual and predicted values.

docs.title: The Training Error and The Test Error¶
docs.text:
In machine learning, it's essential to evaluate how well a model performs. Two common metrics used for this purpose are the training error and the test error:

  • Training Error: This is the error (typically the MSE) of the model on the same data it was trained on. A low training error might indicate that the model fits the training data well, but it doesn't necessarily mean the model will perform well on new, unseen data.

  • Test Error: This is the error of the model on a separate set of data that it hasn't seen during training. It gives a better indication of how the model will perform in real-world scenarios. A model that performs well on the training data but poorly on the test data is likely overfitting.

In a business context, the training error can help in understanding how well the model fits historical data, while the test error can provide insights into how the model might perform on future data.

Let's calculate the training and test errors for a sample linear regression model using a business-related dataset.

docs.title: The Cost Function (Revisited)¶
docs.text:
The cost function, as previously mentioned, quantifies the error between the model's predictions and the actual values. For regression problems, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) is a commonly used cost function. It's crucial to minimize this error during the training process to ensure the model makes accurate predictions.

In a business context, the cost function can be thought of as a measure of how far off our predictions are from the actual outcomes. For instance, if we're predicting monthly sales, a high cost would indicate that our predictions are far from the actual sales figures, which could lead to incorrect business decisions.

Now, let's move on to the next topic.

docs.title: Bias versus Variance (Revisited)¶
docs.text:
Bias and variance are two fundamental concepts in understanding the performance of machine learning models. They represent two types of errors that can occur:

  • Bias: This is the error introduced by approximating a real-world problem, which might be complex, by a too-simple model. High bias can cause the model to miss the relevant relations between features and target outputs, leading to underfitting. In a business context, a high-bias model might consistently make the same type of error, such as consistently underestimating sales by a certain amount.

  • Variance: This is the error introduced by using a model that's too complex. High variance can cause the model to model the random noise in the training data, leading to overfitting. In a business context, a high-variance model might be very sensitive to small fluctuations in the training data, leading to erratic predictions.

The challenge in machine learning is to find the right trade-off between bias and variance. Ideally, we want a model with low bias and low variance, but in practice, there's often a trade-off. Reducing bias might increase variance and vice versa.

In a business scenario, understanding bias and variance is crucial. A model with high bias might lead to consistent errors in decision-making, while a model with high variance might lead to unpredictable and erratic decisions.

Now, let's move on to the next topic.

docs.title: Exercise: Overfitting and Underfitting in Business Sales Prediction¶
docs.text:
Scenario: You are a data scientist at a retail company, and you are tasked with predicting monthly sales based on advertising spend. You decide to use polynomial regression. However, you want to ensure that your model neither overfits nor underfits the data.

Objective: Fit polynomial regression models of varying degrees to the sales data and visualize the results to understand the concepts of overfitting and underfitting.

Let's start by visualizing the provided sales data.

docs.title: Exercise: Understanding the Cost Function in Business¶
docs.text:
Scenario: You are working for a retail company and are tasked with predicting monthly sales based on advertising spend. You've chosen a linear regression model for this task. To evaluate the performance of your model, you decide to compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) as your cost function.

Objective: Calculate the MSE for your linear regression model using both the training and test data. Compare the results to understand the model's performance.

Let's begin by calculating the MSE for the training data.

docs.title: Exercise: Evaluating Model Performance using Training and Test Errors¶
docs.text:
Scenario: You are a data scientist at a retail company. The marketing team wants to understand the performance of the sales prediction model before launching a new advertising campaign. They are particularly interested in knowing how well the model performs on historical data (training data) and how it might perform on future data (test data).

Objective: Calculate the training and test errors for the sales prediction model. Analyze the results to provide insights to the marketing team.

Let's begin by calculating the training and test errors.

The error falls from ≈ 0.58 to ≈ 0.31. Nothing is wrong with the code — the decile is computed from income, the thing we are trying to predict. In a proxy means test you would never have it: if you knew the decile, you would not need the model. The question to ask about every feature is: would I have this value at the moment I need the prediction?

docs.title: Session 4 · The ML Pipeline, in the Right Order¶
docs.text:
The case. You work for a social-policy unit. Programmes must reach poor households, but income is hard to verify: people under-report it, and checking it is expensive. So governments predict welfare from things that are easy to observe — schooling, household size, age. This is called a proxy means test, and Chile's Registro Social de Hogares and Mexico's Progresa are built on it.

Today's question. How well can we predict a household's (log) income per capita from three observable characteristics — and how do we know the number we report is honest?

What you already know (Sessions 1–3): pandas, train/test split, KNN, linear regression, the bias–variance trade-off. What is new today: scaling, Pipeline, k-fold cross-validation, and three kinds of data leakage.

docs.title: 1. Define the population and the target¶
docs.text:
Each row is one household from CASEN 2022. A handful report zero income; the logarithm is not defined there, so we leave them out and say so — every row we drop is a decision.

We model log(income per capita) because income is very skewed: a few households earn a hundred times the median, and on the raw scale they would dominate the error.

docs.title: 2. Split first — before you look at anything else¶
docs.text: The test set is the stand-in for households the model has never seen. From this line on, nothing we decide may use it — not the scaling, not the choice of k, not the choice of features.

docs.title: 3. Recap of Session 3: linear regression and KNN¶
4. New tool #1 — scaling¶
docs.text:
KNN decides who is "near" using distances. Age runs from about 15 to 100, schooling from 0 to 25, household size from 1 to 13. Without scaling, a 10-year age gap counts as much as 10 extra years of schooling — the variable with the widest range dominates the distance just because of its units.

StandardScaler rescales each column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It learns the mean and the standard deviation — so, like a model, it must learn them from the training set only.

docs.title: ✋ Check the worked example from the session page¶
docs.text: The page computes, by hand, the two nearest neighbours of a new household (age 40, 12 years of schooling, 4 members) among four households A–D, with and without scaling. Reproduce it here, and compare the result with your paper version.

docs.title: 5. New tool #2 — the Pipeline¶
docs.text: Fitting the scaler and the model by hand works, but you have to remember the order every time — and in cross-validation you would have to repeat it inside every fold. A Pipeline glues the steps into one object: .fit() fits each step on the data it receives, in order, and .predict() applies them.

docs.title: 6. New tool #3 — k-fold cross-validation, to choose k honestly¶
docs.text:
Which k should we use? The tempting answer — "try several and keep the best test score" — is a leak: the test set would be choosing the model, and its score would no longer be honest.

Instead we split the training set into 5 folds. Each fold takes a turn as a mini-test set while the other 4 train the pipeline. Because the scaler lives inside the pipeline, it is refitted on the 4 training folds every time — no fold ever sees its own validation data.

docs.title: 7. Leakage hunt¶
docs.text: Leakage is any way information that would not be available at prediction time reaches the model. Three cases, on our own data.

docs.title: Leak A — scaling before the split¶
Leak B — a feature built from the target¶
docs.text: CASEN also publishes each household's income decile. It is tempting: it is "just a category".

docs.title: Leak C — choosing the model with the test set¶
docs.text: If we had picked k by looking at test scores, the test score would be the best of many tries — an optimistic number. That is why we chose k with cross-validation on the training set (section 6).

docs.title: One more to keep in mind — the same unit on both sides¶
docs.text: Our rows are households. If the rows were people, members of the same household would land in both train and test, and the model would "recognise" their shared income. Make the unit of analysis the unit you will predict for, or split by group (GroupKFold).

docs.title: 8. With your assistant¶
docs.text:
Here is my scikit-learn code (paste it). Review it for data leakage.
For every transformation, say whether it is fitted before or after the train/test split.
For every feature, say whether it would be available at prediction time in a proxy means test.
List the problems first, then the corrected code.

Then check its answer against this notebook. Did it catch income_decile? Did it flag anything that is not actually a problem?

docs.title: 9. Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Add head_weekly_hours as a fourth feature. What do its missing values mean? (Hint: look at head_activity.) Fill them with .fillna() using the value that matches that meaning. Why is a fixed rule like this safe to apply before the split, while a learned mean would not be?
  2. Repeat the cross-validation with LinearRegression instead of KNN. Which would you choose, and why?
  3. Write two sentences explaining to a policymaker why a model with RMSE 0.31 should not be used.

docs.title: Session 5 · Classification: Who Is Poor?¶
docs.text:
Last session we predicted (log) income per capita and learned to report an honest error with a pipeline and cross-validation.

Today's question. A programme does not pay "a predicted income" — it decides yes or no: does this household get the subsidy? So we predict the class directly: is the household poor?

What is new today: logistic regression as a predictor, the confusion matrix, precision and recall, the decision threshold, the ROC curve and AUC, stratified splits — and how to put categorical variables and missing values inside the pipeline (OneHotEncoder, SimpleImputer, ColumnTransformer).

docs.title: 1. A stratified split, and the "nobody is poor" baseline¶
docs.text: About 23% of households are poor. A random split could, by chance, put a different share in train and test; stratify=y keeps the 23% in both. Then the first baseline: predict "not poor" for everybody.

docs.title: 2. Logistic regression — the model you know from econometrics, used to predict¶
docs.text: In econometrics you used the logit to estimate effects. Here it is the same equation, $P(\text{poor}) = 1 / (1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots)})$, but we judge it by how well it predicts households it has never seen. Start with the three numeric variables from Session 4.

docs.title: ✋ The logit by hand, with one variable¶
docs.text: The page fits $P(\text{poor})$ on years of schooling alone and computes three probabilities by hand. Fit the same model and check your arithmetic.

docs.title: 3. The confusion matrix: two different mistakes¶
docs.text:
predicted not poor predicted poor actually not poor true negative false positive — subsidy to a household that does not need it actually poor false negative — a poor household is left out true positive
  • Recall = of the poor households, what share do we reach? TP / (TP + FN)
  • Precision = of the households we select, what share are actually poor? TP / (TP + FP)

docs.title: 4. Use all the information: categorical variables and missing values in the pipeline¶
docs.text:
Most of what we know about a household is categorical (region, tenure, health insurance…). Models need numbers, so OneHotEncoder turns each category into a 0/1 column. Missing values need a rule, and the rule depends on what missing means:

Column Why it is missing Rule head_weekly_hours the head does not work fill with 0 — not the median! head_job_type the head does not work its own category, "missing" schooling, education, insurance, overcrowding "doesn't know" (rare) median / own category

ColumnTransformer applies a different mini-pipeline to each group of columns. Everything that is learned (medians, categories, scaling) is learned inside the pipeline — on training folds only.

docs.title: 5. The threshold is a policy decision¶
docs.text: .predict() says "poor" when the probability is above 0.5. Nothing says 0.5 is right. Lower the threshold and we reach more poor households (recall ↑) at the price of subsidising more households that are not poor (precision ↓).

docs.title: 6. The ROC curve and AUC: the model across all thresholds¶
docs.text: The ROC curve plots recall (true positive rate) against the false positive rate for every threshold. The AUC summarises it: the probability that a random poor household gets a higher score than a random non-poor one. 0.5 is a coin; 1.0 is perfect.

docs.title: 7. Honest evaluation: stratified cross-validation¶
docs.text: Same idea as Session 4, with folds that each keep the 23% of poor households.

docs.title: 8. Leakage, again: what if we add income?¶
9. Reading the model (carefully)¶
docs.text: Exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios, as in econometrics. But this model was built to predict: the coefficients describe associations among correlated variables, not causal effects.

docs.title: 10. With your assistant¶
docs.text:
I have a logistic regression that predicts whether a household is poor (23% positive class).
Here is my confusion matrix at threshold 0.5: (paste). Explain in plain language what each cell means
for a social programme. Then write code that picks the threshold minimising 3*FN + 1*FP on
cross-validated predictions (not on the test set). Tell me why that last condition matters.

Check: did it use cross_val_predict (or equivalent) rather than the test set to choose the threshold?

docs.title: 11. Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Recompute the cost-minimising threshold with a cost ratio of 1:1 and 5:1. How many more poor households are reached, and at what cost in false positives?
  2. Choose the threshold using cross_val_predict on the training set, then report recall and precision on the test set once. Compare with the threshold chosen on the test set above — which is honest?
  3. Drop region. Does the AUC change? Would a region-blind model be easier to defend politically?
  4. Count the employed heads with missing head_weekly_hours (df.query("head_activity == 'employed'")). Why is 0 the wrong value for them? Propose a better rule, and say whether it must be learned from the training data — and therefore go inside the pipeline.

def gini(p):
    return 2 * p * (1 - p)

def split_impurity(x, y, cut):
    """Weighted Gini of the two groups x <= cut and x > cut."""
    left, right = y[x <= cut], y[x > cut]
    n = len(y)
    return len(left) / n * gini(left.mean()) + len(right) / n * gini(right.mean())

def cost_threshold(p, y_true, fn_cost=3, fp_cost=1):
    """Threshold on a 0.01 grid that minimises fn_cost*FN + fp_cost*FP."""
    ts = np.round(np.arange(0.02, 0.90, 0.01), 2)
    cost = [fn_cost * ((p < t) & (y_true == 1)).sum() + fp_cost * ((p >= t) & (y_true == 0)).sum() for t in ts]
    return ts[int(np.argmin(cost))]


def evaluate(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, cv):
    """CV AUC, a cost-based threshold chosen on training folds, and test-set results."""
    s = cross_validate(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", return_train_score=True)
    oof = cross_val_predict(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
    t = cost_threshold(oof, y_train.to_numpy())
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    yt = y_test.to_numpy()
    return {"train AUC": s["train_score"].mean(), "CV AUC": s["test_score"].mean(),
            "CV sd": s["test_score"].std(), "test AUC": roc_auc_score(yt, p), "threshold": t,
            "recall": recall_score(yt, p >= t), "precision": precision_score(yt, p >= t),
            "cost 3FN+FP": 3 * ((p < t) & (yt == 1)).sum() + ((p >= t) & (yt == 0)).sum()}

def cost_threshold(p, y_true, fn_cost=3, fp_cost=1): """Threshold on a 0.01 grid that minimises fn_cost*FN + fp_cost*FP.""" ts = np.round(np.arange(0.02, 0.90, 0.01), 2) cost = [fn_cost * ((p < t) & (y_true == 1)).sum() + fp_cost * ((p >= t) & (y_true == 0)).sum() for t in ts] return ts[int(np.argmin(cost))] def evaluate(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, cv): """CV AUC, a cost-based threshold chosen on training folds, and test-set results.""" s = cross_validate(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", return_train_score=True) oof = cross_val_predict(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1] t = cost_threshold(oof, y_train.to_numpy()) model.fit(X_train, y_train) p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] yt = y_test.to_numpy() return {"train AUC": s["train_score"].mean(), "CV AUC": s["test_score"].mean(), "CV sd": s["test_score"].std(), "test AUC": roc_auc_score(yt, p), "threshold": t, "recall": recall_score(yt, p >= t), "precision": precision_score(yt, p >= t), "cost 3FN+FP": 3 * ((p < t) & (yt == 1)).sum() + ((p >= t) & (yt == 0)).sum()} models = { "Logit (Session 5)": logit, "Tree (depth 4)": Pipeline([("pre", pre_tree), ("clf", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42))]), "Random forest": Pipeline([("pre", pre_tree), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier( n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42))]), "Gradient boosting": Pipeline([("pre", pre_tree), ("clf", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42))]), } results = pd.DataFrame({name: evaluate(m, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, cv) for name, m in models.items()}).T results.round(3) Out[11]: train AUC CV AUC CV sd test AUC threshold recall precision cost 3FN+FP Logit (Session 5) 0.789 0.781 0.009 0.794 0.26 0.680 0.454 1540.0 Tree (depth 4) 0.757 0.746 0.009 0.767 0.24 0.682 0.446 1560.0 Random forest 0.903 0.797 0.007 0.814 0.24 0.745 0.460 1421.0 Gradient boosting 0.910 0.798 0.007 0.815 0.20 0.788 0.439 1422.0

The ensembles gain about 0.02 AUC over the logit, and at their own cost-minimising thresholds the policy cost falls by roughly 8%. That is real, but it is not a revolution. The depth-4 tree is slightly worse than the logit, but anyone can read it.

Importance says what the model uses to predict, not what causes poverty. Working fewer hours is associated with poverty, partly because poverty and unemployment share causes. And when two variables carry the same information (schooling years and education level), shuffling one costs little because the other covers for it.

docs.title: Session 6 · Trees and Ensembles¶
docs.text:
Last session the logit predicted poverty with a test AUC of 0.79, but missed many poor households.

Today's question. Can a more flexible model find the poor households the logit misses, and what do we give up in exchange?

What is new today: decision trees (DecisionTreeClassifier, Gini impurity, max_depth, min_samples_leaf, plot_tree, export_text), bagging and the bootstrap, random forests (RandomForestClassifier, out-of-bag error), gradient boosting (HistGradientBoostingClassifier), cross_val_predict, and permutation importance.

docs.title: 1. The reference: the Session 5 logit¶
docs.text: Every model today is compared with this one, on the same folds and the same test set.

docs.title: 2. One question at a time: the Gini impurity¶
docs.text:
A tree splits the households into two groups with a yes/no question, then splits each group again. To choose the question, it measures how mixed each group is. With a share $p$ of poor households, the Gini impurity is

$$G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1-p)$$

It is 0 when a group is pure (all poor or none poor) and 0.5 when it is a 50/50 mix. A split is good if the weighted average impurity of the two groups is much lower than the impurity before it.

docs.title: 3. A first tree¶
docs.text: Trees need numbers too, so we still one-hot encode the categories, but we drop the scaler.

docs.title: 4. How deep? Overfitting again¶
docs.text: Each extra level doubles the number of groups. Deep enough, every leaf holds a handful of households and the tree memorises the training set, like KNN with k = 1.

docs.title: 5. Many trees: bagging and random forests¶
docs.text:
A single deep tree is unstable: change a few households and the questions change. The fix is to grow many trees and average them.

  1. Bootstrap: draw a sample of the same size with replacement from the training set (some households appear twice, about a third not at all).
  2. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): fit one tree per bootstrap sample and average their predicted probabilities. Each tree overfits differently; the average cancels much of the noise.
  3. Random forest: bagging plus one more trick. At each split, a tree may only look at a random subset of the variables (max_features), so the trees disagree more, and the average improves.

The households a tree never saw (its out-of-bag sample) give a free validation score.

docs.title: 6. Trees that correct each other: gradient boosting¶
docs.text: Boosting grows trees in sequence. Each new, small tree is fitted to what the current model still gets wrong, and is added with a small weight (learning_rate). After many rounds, many weak trees add up to a strong model. Too many rounds overfit, so HistGradientBoostingClassifier holds out 10% of the training data and stops early when that held-out score stops improving.

docs.title: 7. The race, done properly¶
docs.text: To compare models fairly we need the same steps for every model, so we write them once, as a function (that is today's assistant skill). The threshold is chosen with cross_val_predict: out-of-fold probabilities on the training set, never the test set.

docs.title: 8. What does the forest rely on? Permutation importance¶
docs.text: Impurity importance (feature_importances_) adds up how much each one-hot column reduced the Gini. It is computed on training data and favours variables with many possible cut points. Permutation importance asks a cleaner question on the test set: if I shuffle this column, so it carries no information, how much AUC do we lose?

docs.title: 9. Accuracy vs. explanation¶
docs.text: A household excluded from a programme can ask why. With the depth-3 tree the answer is a short chain of questions. With 300 trees there is no short answer. Whether 0.02 of AUC is worth that is a decision for the programme, and your job is to put both numbers on the table.

docs.title: 10. With your assistant: refactor a script into functions¶
docs.text:
Here is my notebook code that evaluates four classifiers (paste sections 1-7).
Refactor it into two functions: cost_threshold(p, y, fn_cost, fp_cost) and
evaluate(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, cv) -> dict.
Keep the results identical. The threshold must be chosen with out-of-fold predictions on the
training set only. Add a docstring to each function and nothing else.

Check: run the old and the new code and compare the table number by number. A refactor that changes a result is a bug, even if the new number looks better.

docs.title: 11. Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Change the cost ratio to 5:1 in cost_threshold. Which model wins now, and how many more poor households does it reach?
  2. Fit a random forest with n_estimators = 10, 50, 300. How do the CV AUC and the run time change?
  3. Write the depth-3 tree as a one-page "scorecard" a municipal officer could apply with pen and paper. Which household in the test set would be hardest to explain?

def preprocessor(cols):
    """The Session 5 preprocessing, restricted to the columns in `cols`."""
    num, hours, cat = [c for c in cols if c in NUM], [c for c in cols if c in HOURS], [c for c in cols if c in CAT]
    parts = []
    if num:

    if hours:
        parts.append(("hours", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=0), StandardScaler()), hours))

Greedy selection picks one of two correlated variables and ignores the other. That says redundant, not irrelevant.

def penalised_logit(C, l1_ratio):
    """l1_ratio = 0 -> Ridge, 1 -> LASSO, in between -> Elastic Net."""
    solver = "liblinear" if l1_ratio in (0, 1) else "saga"
    if NEW_API:
        return LogisticRegression(C=C, l1_ratio=l1_ratio, solver=solver, max_iter=5000, random_state=0)
    penalty = {0: "l2", 1: "l1"}.get(l1_ratio, "elasticnet")
    extra = {"l1_ratio": l1_ratio} if penalty == "elasticnet" else {}
    return LogisticRegression(C=C, penalty=penalty, solver=solver, max_iter=5000, random_state=0, **extra)

With 300 households the unpenalised logit has 76 coefficients to estimate from about 70 poor households. It fits the noise, and the penalty cuts that variance. With all the data the gap disappears. This is the bias–variance trade-off from Session 3 again: the penalty adds a little bias to remove a lot of variance, and that trade is worth making when variance is the bigger problem.
