The short form gives up a little AUC and saves 11 questions per household visit. Whether that trade is worth it depends on the cost of a visit, the risk of manipulation and the cost of each error. That is a policy decision, but now it can be made with numbers on the table.

docs.title: Session 7 · Selection and Shrinkage: How Short Can the Form Be?¶
docs.text:
So far our poverty model uses 19 variables: 19 questions a social worker must ask, record and verify in every household visit.

Today's question. Every question costs interview time, can be gamed by applicants, and must be checked. Which variables do we really need? A shorter form that predicts almost as well is a policy win.

What is new today: forward stepwise selection, penalised logistic regression (Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net), the penalty strength C = 1/λ, the regularisation path, and choosing the penalty by cross-validation.

docs.title: 1. The preprocessing, as a function of which questions we keep¶
docs.text: Same rules as Session 5, but now the list of columns changes from model to model, so we wrap the ColumnTransformer in a small function.

docs.title: 2. Forward stepwise selection: build the form one question at a time¶
docs.text:
Best subset selection would try every possible form: with 19 questions that is 2¹⁹ ≈ 524,000 models. Forward stepwise is the greedy shortcut: start with no questions; at each step add the one question that raises the cross-validated AUC the most.

We select questions (raw variables), not dummy columns: a form cannot ask "region = Maule?" without asking the region. scikit-learn's SequentialFeatureSelector works on the columns of the final matrix (the dummies), so we write the loop ourselves, with one pipeline per candidate set. It takes about a minute.

docs.title: 3. Penalised regression: shrink instead of choosing¶
docs.text:
Selection is all-or-nothing. Shrinkage keeps every variable but adds a price for large coefficients to the quantity the model minimises:

$$\text{log-loss}(\beta) + \lambda \cdot \text{penalty}(\beta)$$

Method Penalty Effect Ridge (L2) $\sum_j \beta_j^2$ shrinks all coefficients towards 0, none exactly 0 LASSO (L1) $\sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert$ shrinks, and sets some coefficients exactly to 0 Elastic Net a mix of both sparse like LASSO, more stable with correlated variables

In scikit-learn the strength is C = 1/λ: small C = strong penalty. Because the penalty compares coefficients with each other, all variables must be on the same scale, which is why the StandardScaler stays in the pipeline.

⚠️ scikit-learn's LogisticRegression() is already Ridge with C = 1 by default. The Session 5 model was slightly penalised all along. Econometrics software (Stata, statsmodels) does not penalise by default.

docs.title: A version trap¶
docs.text: scikit-learn 1.8 changed how you ask for LASSO: penalty="l1" became l1_ratio=1. Older versions, still common on Colab, silently ignore l1_ratio unless penalty="elasticnet", and so fit a Ridge without telling you. This helper works on both:

docs.title: 4. The LASSO path: from no variables to all of them¶
docs.text: We fit the LASSO for 40 values of C, from a very strong penalty (C = 0.001) to a weak one (C = 10), and record the coefficients, the CV AUC, and how many questions still have at least one non-zero coefficient.

docs.title: 5. Ridge vs LASSO vs Elastic Net on the full form¶
6. When does shrinkage pay off? When data is scarce¶
docs.text: Imagine a pilot survey in one province: a few hundred households, the same 76 columns. We train on random subsamples of the training set and evaluate on the (full) test set.

docs.title: 8. With your assistant: debugging, not guessing¶
docs.text:
I fit LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1, solver="liblinear", C=0.03) inside a Pipeline on Colab,
expecting a LASSO, but none of the 76 coefficients is exactly zero. My scikit-learn version is
(paste sklearn.__version__). Diagnose the cause. Show me the evidence: which line of the
documentation for MY version explains it, and a two-line check I can run to confirm.

Check: does it ask for (or use) your version before answering? Does it give you a check you can run (count coef_ == 0), or only a confident explanation?

docs.title: 9. Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Remove the StandardScaler from the numeric pipeline and refit the 1-SE LASSO. Which coefficients change most, and why does the penalty now treat head_age unfairly?
  2. Continue the forward selection to all 19 questions. At which step does the CV AUC stop changing in the third decimal? Does that agree with the LASSO's ranking of variables?
  3. Your short form keeps region. Refit it without region: how much CV AUC do you lose? Write three sentences for a ministry explaining one advantage and one risk of a region-blind targeting rule.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2)) ax[0].plot(choose["k"], choose["inertia"], "o-"); ax[0].set_title("Inertia (elbow)"); ax[0].set_xlabel("k") ax[1].plot(choose["k"], choose["silhouette"], "o-"); ax[1].set_title("Silhouette (higher = better)"); ax[1].set_xlabel("k") plt.tight_layout()

An honest reading: there is no sharp elbow, and every silhouette is low (0.21 to 0.25). Households form a continuum, not well-separated islands. That is normal with social data, and it is worth saying out loud.

The two criteria do not agree perfectly. The silhouette is highest at k = 3. But k = 3 puts families with and without children in one group (57% with children), which is exactly the distinction a family programme cares about. Going from 3 to 4 clusters still cuts inertia by 12,100, while from 4 to 5 the gain drops to 8,300. We take k = 4, and we say why. Choosing k is a judgement call, and you should defend it with numbers and with the use you will give the segments.

The overcrowded families are poor at 40%, almost twice the sample's 23%. Working adults without children are at 16%. The algorithm never saw the label, yet the segments it found differ a lot in poverty.

docs.title: Session 8 · Unlabeled Data: PCA and Clustering¶
docs.text:
So far every model had an answer to learn from: income (Sessions 3–4) or the label poor (Sessions 5–7). That is supervised learning.

Today's question. Programmes are designed for profiles, such as older people living alone, young families with children or overcrowded households. They are not designed for a single score. What types of households are there, if we never tell the algorithm who is poor? This is unsupervised learning: there is no target, only the features.

What is new today: PCA (principal components, explained variance, loadings, scores), k-means (inertia, the elbow, the silhouette), hierarchical clustering with a dendrogram, and cluster profiling.

The rule for today: income and poor are never inputs. We look at poverty only after the clusters exist, to describe them.

docs.title: 1. Choose what describes a household¶
docs.text:
Clustering finds groups in the variables you give it. Choosing them is a substantive decision, not a technicality. We pick ten variables about who lives in the household and how. Each one is something a programme designer would care about, and none of them is income:

  • the head of household: age, years of schooling, weekly hours worked (0 if not working), female head
  • the household: size, children under 18, people over 60, rural, owns the home, overcrowded

Categorical columns become 0/1 with plain pandas comparisons. One column needs care: head_weekly_hours is missing both for heads who do not work (they get 0) and for 87 working heads who did not know their hours (CASEN codes that as −88 in the raw survey; the course file already turns it into missing). For those 87, 0 would be wrong, so we give them the median hours of the people who work.

docs.title: 2. Standardise first¶
docs.text:
Both PCA and k-means work with distances and variances. Age has a standard deviation of about 16 years, while has_children has one of about 0.5. Without scaling, age and hours would decide everything. StandardScaler puts every column at mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

There is no train/test split today. We are describing the data, not predicting new households, so there is no test error to protect. Section 9 comes back to what "validation" can mean here.

docs.title: 3. PCA with two variables: see the idea¶
docs.text: Take just age and schooling. Older heads of household in Chile had less schooling, so the two are negatively correlated. PCA rotates the axes. PC1 is the direction along which the cloud is most spread out, and PC2 is perpendicular to it.

docs.title: 5. k-means, by hand first¶
docs.text:
k-means looks for k groups whose members are close to their group's centre (the centroid). It alternates two steps until nothing changes:

  1. Assign each household to its nearest centroid.
  2. Update each centroid to the mean of its households.

Here is the six-household example from the session page, checked with numpy:

docs.title: 6. k-means on the households, and how to choose k¶
docs.text:
Inertia is the total squared distance from each household to its centroid. It always falls as k grows: with k = 15,000, every household is its own cluster and inertia is 0. So we look for an elbow, the point where adding clusters stops helping much.

The silhouette compares, for each household, the distance to its own cluster with the distance to the nearest other cluster. It runs from −1 to 1, and higher means better-separated clusters. It is slow on 15,000 rows, so we compute it on a random 3,000.

docs.title: Local minima: why n_init matters¶
docs.text: k-means starts from random centroids (chosen with the k-means++ rule) and only ever moves "downhill". So it can get stuck in a solution that is good locally but not the best one. Watch k = 4 started from five different seeds, one run each:

docs.title: 7. Profile the clusters¶
docs.text: A cluster is just a number until you describe it. We average the original (unscaled) variables by cluster.

docs.title: 8. Now — and only now — look at poverty¶
9. Results depend on your choices: scaling and variables¶
A rare 0/1 variable can grab a cluster¶
docs.text: Only about 4% of households are overcrowded. After standardisation, a 1 in that column becomes a very large number:

docs.title: 10. Hierarchical clustering: a second opinion¶
docs.text: Agglomerative clustering starts with every household on its own and repeatedly merges the two closest groups. With Ward linkage, "closest" means the merge that increases within-cluster variance the least, the same objective as k-means. The dendrogram shows the whole merge history. Cutting it at a height gives clusters. It needs all pairwise distances, so we use 500 households.

docs.title: 11. With your assistant: review the plot, not just the code¶
docs.text:
I clustered 15,000 Chilean households into 4 groups with k-means on 10 standardised variables
(listed here). Write code for (1) a scatter of the first two PCA scores coloured by cluster, with
the explained variance in each axis label, and (2) a bar chart of the cluster profiles in the
original units. Then describe each cluster in one sentence.

Then check:

  • Do the axis labels show the real explained variance (31% and 15%)?
  • Did it plot scaled or unscaled values in the profile chart, and did it say which?
  • Is every claim in its description backed by a number in your profile table?
  • Did it call the clusters "natural types", or claim they cause poverty?

docs.title: 12. Exercises¶
docs.text:
1. Remove overcrowded from the features and rerun k = 4. What happens to the 579 overcrowded households? Which profile would you show a policymaker, and why?
  2. Run k-means on the first three PCA scores instead of the ten standardised variables. Do you get similar profiles? What did you lose and gain?
  3. Pick k = 6. Describe the two new clusters. Are they worth a separate programme?
